The House in Committee on Bill No. 59, respecting the Toronto, Niagara and Western Railway Company.-Mr. Currie. Mr, Blondin in the Chair.

The hon. member for
Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) yesterday discussed this Bill at some length and moved certain amendments. Unrevised 'Hansard' got it mixed up in some way, and set forth that the objection of the hon. gentleman was to clause 5, but I think it was clause 7 to which he had reference.

My hon. friend from South Renfrew is quite correct; the Chairman of the Railway made the necessary corrections in unrevised ' Hansard.'
On section 7-construction of railway:

We all regret, I am sure, the reason which made it necessary for the hon. member for Lincoln to speak on this Bill in advance of it being discussed in Committee of the Whole. No one regrets the hon. gentleman's ill-health more than I, and trust that the Chairman of the Railway 'Committee may be back here soon in his accustomed good health. I think the hon. gentleman has an obsession with regard to the importance of this section. This Bill was on two occasions before the Standing Orders Committee, once after it had been discussed by the Railway Committee, and it was held that these amendments would be quite proper in the Bill. In the Railway Committee, the corporation counsel of Toronto and others were heard; the matter was fully and thoroughly discussed, and on a vote of 14 to 25, clauses 5, 6 and 7 were, on my motion, added to the Bill. Clause 7 is not a new clause. The clauses were all designed to safeguard the city of Toronto. Toronto has its difficulties with regard to railways entering the city, and it is now in the midst of solving them. For years past the city has

been endeavouring to wipe out all level crossings, and to-day it is contributing over four million dollars to assist the railways to that end. Toronto .asks no special privileges, but, owing to the circumstances of the case and the congestion of traffic, the problem of level crossings in Toronto is very different from that of level crossings in country districts or in smaller towns. The level crossing is now practically a thing of the past in Toronto. The railways along the entire waterfront from the extreme east to the extreme west are now being put on viaducts, and other means have been taken to remove level crossings, *so that it may be said that the city has in hand a complete and final solution of the level crossing difficulty. There soon will not be a level crossing in the south part of Toronto, and the city is now embarking on a scheme for the removal of level crossings in the northern, part of the city. Just where this railway has its right of way, adjacent to the Canadian Pacific railway tracks, the city has, at an expense of between one and two million dollars, contributed towards aiding the Canadian Pacific railway to raise their tracks on a viaduct from Yonge street to a point west of Dufferin street, over two and a half miles in length. The right of way of this road' runs alongside of that.
The chairman of the Railway Committee talks about vested rights, but this company has no vested rights. The hon. gentleman was quite mistaken when he said that this company had undertaken .certain work in the city of Toronto. They have not removed one shovelful of earth, they have not graded a rod, and they have not laid a tie. All they have done is to acquire the right of way, for about two and a half miles, which crosses on the level some twenty-four or twenty-five streets in the city. All that the amendment asks is that this company be not permitted, without the consent of the city, to cross these streets on the level. This company was incorporated in 1903, eleven years ago, and, though it has had various extensions of time since, up to the present they have not done anything in the city of Toronto. They were granted extensions in 1904, 1906 and 1909, and they are now asking for a further extension. The uncontradicted evidence produced before the Railway Committee was that they had done no work outside of Toronto. It is true that they formed some combination with the Toronto

Suburban Railway Company, and that that company has done certain work outside of the city, but no work has been done by this company under its charter either inside or outside of the city of Toronto except the acquiring of a certain right of way. As I have said, they cross twenty-four or twenty-five streets in the course of the two and a half miles which they have already purchased, and they may go through two and a half miles more of the city and cross fifty streets. It is now asked, in view of the fact that Toronto is now spending millions of dollars with a view to removing its level crossings, that this railway should not be allowed to do ^.what other railways are not allowed to do. This same provision has been put in railway Bills during the last three or four years. While the hon. member for South Wellington presided over the Railway Committee, similar clauses, identical in language, were inserted in at least three different railway Bills. In 1910 a similar clause was put in Acts respecting the Western Central Railway Company and the Toronto Eastern Railway Company, and in 1911 in the Act relating to the Hamilton, Waterloo and Guelph Railway Company. Thi3 clause, therefore, has become a practically standard one, as applied to railways getting a charter into the city of Toronto, and similar clauses have been accepted by the committee from 1910 up to the present time, uniformly and without exception. It is interesting to note that the railway company is quite satisfied with these provisions. In their opinion, they are suffering no hardship. In the Railway Committee they agreed to accept these safeguarding provisions, and there can be no objection, so far as I can see, why they should not be inserted in the Bill.
The Chairman of the Railway Committee yesterday protested against the insertion of this safeguarding clause in the Bill because of vested rights. There are no vested rights in this matter; these people have had a charter for eleven years and have done nothing. When they got their charter, the district through which they were to go was almost entirely uninhabited; it was then part of the suburbs or outskirts of the city of Toronto. Now that very district is as near the centre of the city of Toronto geographically, east and west, as any line can be. If the wish of the hon. member for Lincoln is to prevail, they are to be permitted now to lay a railway, ten or eleven years after obtaining
their charter, through a district which is in the centre of the city of Toronto. The reasons for safeguarding the people of that district have arisen since the charter was granted. Vested rights, if there are any, are in the citizens of Toronto through which city that road runs. The right of way bought and paid for by the company is to-day worth many times what they paid for it, and they are suffering no loss or injury in that respect; nor can they by any possibility be subject to any loss or damage in connection with their investment in Toronto. In view of the fact that the committee during the last four years deliberately approved these sections respecting railways entering Toronto, I do not see why at this late date we should make any change, especially in view of the fact that the railway people themselves are perfectly satisfied to accept these provisions. I ask the committee to pass the Bill as it came from the Railway Committee and the other committees of the House through which it went.

The point raised in connection with this amendment is an exceedingly important one, especially to those who reside outside of the city of Toronto. A very large portion of the people of Ontario desire to go to Toronto and to have every reasonable means afforded to them of obtaining access to the heart of that city. It so happens-and, I think, has happened during the last eight or ten years-'that whenever railway proposals affecting the	city of Toronto	come
before this House or before the Railway Committee, Toronto representatives are inclined to insist upon terms 'being inserted in the charters which are not accorded to any other cities in the province of Ontario or, so far as I am awaTe, in the Dominion of Canada. The question may possibly arise in the city of Toronto by reason of the fact that their street franchise, which is now held by the Toronto Railway Company, will expire in the course of six or seven years and they probably want to control their own streets at the expiration of that time. But apart altogether from the question of Toronto's rights in the matter, the people of Ontario also have their rights. Until the year 1910 I do not believe that any charter was ever granted in this House containing such a provision as section 7 of the present Bill. The reason why similar clauses were inserted in charters to which my hon. friend referred was that they were new undertakings. They had no previous rights; they

had never spent a dollar and the committee took the view that as they had never expended any money nor committed themselves to any great extent, they should be brought face to face with the fact that Toronto did not want any ^railways on or across their streets until the question of their street franchise was decided. That was, perhaps, a reasonable view and in the Bills enumerated by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, clause 7 was inserted. But the Tesult was that these railways were blocked. The Toronto, Hamilton and Waterloo railway, which my hon. friend has mentioned, was granted a charter containing a clause similar to section 7 of this Bill. It was supported by capitalists. A gentleman who. attended the sittings of the committee where the Bill was very strongly opposed was His Honour the present Lieutenant Governor of Ontario. I have been assured by him that clause 7 was the blocking clause which really meant that the enterprise could not enter the city of Toronto except by tunnel, and the cost of that would have been so great that the project was finally abandoned.
But this railway, the Toronto, Niagara and Western, is an entirely different proposition. It obtained its charter, I think, in 1903 or 1904, and it has had its time extended once or twice. In the year 1909, it began active operations, or undertook the work of construction w'ith a definite end in view. For that purpose the company went to the Railway Board, as the law says they shall do, and had their plans approved into the city of Toronto. Their application to the Railway Board was made in December 1909, and I have in my hand the order made by the board on that occasion. It was made in the presence of counsel for the city of Toronto, and for the Grand Trunk .railway and for the Canadian Pacific railway. The company was authorized to cross streets in the city of Toronto to enable them to get at the terminal points they desired. That was only a preliminary order of the board. A subsequent order, made on the 10th of December, approves their plans of location of their line in the city of Toronto, crossing the twenty-four or twenty-five streets mentioned by my hon. friend from South Toronto. Then it was that the company expended its money. They did not take the streets, but they bought their own right of way immediately adjoining the Canadian Pacific railway to their terminal point. They paid a large sum of money, something in the neighbourhood of $100,000 or $125,000. Part of that money was paid to the city of Tor-

onto itself for land which the city sold to the railway company. That location w'as approved by the Minister and approved by the board and they have held that location ever since, being in this respect in the same position as is the Canadian Pacific railway at this moment. Having that entrance, they immediately lookqd around for other points to *which their railway might go in the province oif Ontario. Their charters were from time to time extended-very much extended. They have the right to run from Toronto to Niagara, from Hamilton to Brantford, and on to Windsor; also through the counties of Peel, Halton, Wellington, Waterloo, Perth, 'and I think, Middlesex and Lamibton. The road now under construction is from the western 'boundary of the city of Toronto to the city of Guelph. They have bought all the right of way.
If I may be allowed, *the bon. gentleman, in the committee was aware of the fact that it was stated that it [DOT]was not this railway that was building from Toronto to Guelph, but another railway.
I will explain that: it is their money anyway.
No.

Perhaps I can explain that too. They have done their grading on a part of the road-I may say the distance from Toronto to Guelph iis fifty miles. They have bought the right of way through the city of Guelph, and between Guelph and Berlin, and I believe they 'have surveyors out between Berlin and Stratford. Now, we in this House gave them power, not to amalgamate with other railways, tout a peculiar power-power to invest in the stocks of other companies. This Toronto, Niagara and Western Railway Company, under the power we gave them in 1909, did invest in the stock of the Toronto and Suburban Railway Company, and the stock of that railway is to-day owned toy the Toronto, Niagara and Western. The bonds which were sold were the Toronto and Suburban bonds now owned and controlled by the applicant company in the present case, and they obtained their money and went on to construct their road. The building is still going on, and ultimately, I believe, the road on the northern line will extend to Stratford, and perhaps through to Sarnia. On the southern branch it is now at N'agara Falls, it has purchased the right of way to Brantford, and I believe it is graded through the city of Brantford and

the intention is to go on to Windsor-thus making a very extensive system of radial lines in western Ontario. They have spent about <a quarter of a million dollars, I believe. But the whole enterprise is being held up through want of an entrance in the city of Toronto, and if clause seven, as it is printed in this Bill stands, that railway will never get an entrance into the city of Toronto. The Board of Railway Commissioners in the order which they made, took care of the rights of the city of Toronto, placing this company on the same plane as the Canadian Pacific railway. The order of the board quoted last night by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. .Lancaster), is as follows:
One order may go In these twenty-five applications. I think one order will cover the whole of them. They may all be consolidated and one order issued in these terms. Authority given to applicants to construct across the streets mentioned, subject to the following conditions:
1.	That if the tracks of the Canadian Pacific railway are at any future time elevated, then the tracks of the applicants shall be likewise elevated along the course of the line where the right of way lie adjacent to each other, upon such terms as the board may direct.
2.	Protection to be provided at such crossings as the chief engineer of the hoard may require before the road is opened for traffic, and if protection is recommended at crossings that any other road is interested in, then the apportionment of the cost of such protection is reserved.
There is the authority of the board placing the Toronto, Niagara and Western upon the same plane as the Canadian Pacific railway. Now, the Canadian Pacific railway has not elevated its tracks.
Excuse me, the Canadian Pacific railway has elevated its tracks.
In North Toronto, where this road is?
For two and a half miles from Yonge street westwards.
Then, the city of Toronto is absolutely protected without clause 7, because they cannot construct without elevating these tracks.

Taking into consideration that the Canadian Pacific railway has elevated its tracks, and that the order of the Railway Board says that this company shall do the same as the Canadian Pacific Tailway, and the clause in the Bill being merely to provide the same in effect, I do not see what objection there can be to the clause.

The clause in the Bill
gives the power to the city engineer absolutely to prohibit the line-
No.

Read the clause:
Unless with the consent of the city of Toronto expressed by by-law the railway of the company shall not be constructed along, upon, above or below any highway as defined by the Railway Act, but notwithstanding anything in this section the railway of the company may be constructed across any such highway, or along or across any easement acquired for public works in the said city, but only above or below such highway or easement, and only after the levels, plans and specifications thereof are approved by the engineer, for the time being, of the said city, or such engineer as may be appointed for that purpose, and the engineer for the time being of the company, and in the event of the said engineers failing to agree, by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
Now, if the Canadian Pacific railway has elevated its track where they are adjacent to the right of way of the Toronto, Niaga/ra and Western, there is no necessity for the clause, because the order of the board provides that this company's tracks also shall be elevated.

The railway does not go
alongside the Canadian Pacific railway for the whole of its length through the city. Is the hon. gentleman going to have it go on the level in these parts?

The pairts where it is
not adjacent to the Canadian Pacific railway. Now, my information is not the information I have been given by hon. gentlemen opposite, that the Canadian Pacific railway has elevated its tracks.
I know it.

A portion of the tracks have been elevated, I know; but there is a large portion of the track that has not been elevated, and it is being operated, and the city of Toronto is not offering any serious objection; and in this c?ase the city of Toronto got our money. Part of the money we paid for right of way was paid into the coffers of the city of Toronto.

I am rather surprised to hear the hon. gentleman express his ownership in this Bill. I have the Bill in my name, and I certainly have not a cent _ invested. It is very unusual for a member to come into this House and promote a Bill, stating that he has an interest in it in that manner.

Yes, as a resident of the province of Ontario desiring to enter the city of Toronto as freely as we enter other cities in Canada, I have an interest in it; and if such legislation is to be passed for the city of Toronto, it should be passed also for the cities of Brantford, Hamilton, Guelph and the other cities of the Dominion. Toronto should not have the exclusive right to say what railways shall come in or what shall not. The clause is a useless clause, if the Canadian Pacific railway has elevated its tracks because you have the order of the Board then to compel others. If the Canadian Pacific railway has not elevated its tracks-and I am still of the opinion that it has not for the entire distance-you have no right to stop these people coming. It is all right for the hon. member for South Toronto to say the land they bought is worth more to-day than when they bought it. That is problematical. I know some people who have land in Toronto who do not think it is worth what they paid for it, and they bought it within the last two or three years. This is a narrow strip of land not saleable except for railway purposes. But this company comes here having paid the city of Toronto and the private owners its money, having its plans approved on the order of the Railway Commission; and still because they ask time to complete their road the committee has said: no, we will block you at the city of Toronto. What use is the road to the rest of the province if it is to be blocked at the western limits of the city of Toronto? We do not want to transfer there from this railway to a street railway or one of the other railways. The Toronto, Niagara and Western Railway Company cannot do a street railway business through the streets of Toronto. That is provided against by another clause-clause 5. All the railway company want is a terminal point within the city where they can discharge their outside passengers and freight. The point in' the Railway Committee was not argued very fully; the vote was a small one, only forty members being represented by the vote. The chairman and the minister were present, but expressed no opinion.
The chairman expressed many opinions.

He left me a letter which he said I might read to the House, but I do not think it becomes necessary to read it. The whole truth of the matter is, so far as the vote is concerned that the

hon. member for North Simcoe, in whose name the Bill stood, accepted certain suggestions of the city of Toronto. That changed the opinion of the whole committee, and after the hon. member accepted	the amendment	of the
member	for South Toronto a great
many who otherwise would have voted to exclude section 7 either did not vote or voted against its exclusion. But to my mind it is nothing but an outrage that those of us who live in the outlying counties, who desire to go to Toronto, cannot enter the city without getting off at the western boundary or taking another line in. We should be entitled to go in on this radial road. This railway runs within 200 yards of the house where I live. I know how convenient it is to me and to many people between Guelph and Toronto and so on to the city of Berlin. For these reasons I submit that the resolution offered by the chairman of the Railway Committee should be agreed to and that clause 7 should be stricken out.

This road goes
through the constituency which I represent. Ten or twelve years ago we had a population there of some ten thousand. Now the population is a good deal over one hundred thousand. At the time the first Act of Incorporation was given, as was said here this afternoon, there was no population to any extent, not even a suburban population. Now it is largely built up. There are certain things incidental to a railway charter. If you got a charter thirteen years under certain conditions then prevailing, it does not follow that i;f you fail to take advantage of the privilege granted you, the rights you then got must continue.
That is only four years ago.

Twelve years ago they got their first charter. They did not act on it. The city has grown and we are trying now in Canada to do away with level crossings, even in the country. Nobody took a more active part than the chairman of the Railway Committe in the fight to secure the abolition of level crossings in connection with the city of St. Catharines, in his own riding. Toronto has become congested as a city and it has gone to great expense to elevate the railway tracks. It is elevating them at the water front at a joint expense of millions of dollars. Now in the upper portion of the city at an expenditure

of millions it is doing the same thing. I think we laid down the principle that all railroads in the city must be elevated, especially those that are to be built hereafter. We get nothing for our policy of trying to do away with level crossings if all those that come along now may make conditions worse after the expenditures we have made to remove this trouble. It is true that the Canadian Pacific railway today is being elevated at the north and where it adjoins this railroad; but this road goes further where it is not adjacent to the Canadian Pacific railway and therefore we will have the evil of a railway coming in to the congested streets of a city with insecure protection to the public. The very same people who have this charter, as I believe, the Canadian Northern railway, recently got legislation to enter the city of Montreal. They come into Montreal by an expensive tunnel; but when they come to the city they were compelled to elevate their tracks and that is only in the last two or three years. The city of Montreal came to this House, represented by their mayor, and made the argument 'before our committee, and practically everything of the Canadian Northern railway is now elevated entering Montreal. I believe that in the public in-'terest this road should elevate its track, but it certainly should consult the city as to its entrance. If they cannot agree they can go, as the Bill provides, to the Railway Commission for relief. In the country we should try and abolish the 'level crossing; certainly we ought to stop it in the city. We are paying liberally to have it stopped and after spending that money if we cannot get relief we expect we might as well have kept our money and have the whole city grid-ironed with street railways on the level. The city itself hopes in a short time to give a tube entrance for all radial lines and I hope by the time this railway is constructed there will be a tube provided for their entrance. One of the great menaces of city life to-day is the destruction of human life, the number of people who are run down by street cars, automobiles and railways makes it a serious risk, and if we are to have railways coming into the city in a congested portion of Toronto there will be great danger to life; it will cost the company as much in the long run even if we do give them the privilege to come in on the level now. After ten years they would have to elevate at their own expense, and it is far better for the city and for the company that that should be done now for
the safeguarding of public life. Safety first is everything in these things. We are making it more unsafe to go into the city, and we are interfering in a way with the right the city of Toronto has to control its own street railway franchises or underground franchises, whatever they may happen to be. Toronto wants to have a high-class city railway service owned by the public. It may take seven years more, or it may take only one year, but the moment the people own the railway the city of Toronto will be prepared to give, on terms, a first-class underground or elevated service for every railway that wants to come in. The city is prepared to put in tubes to give a first-class local service, and to provide the amplest accommodation for every radial to come into the city. We are also forcing another idea; that is, the joint usage of these elevated roads. Why should one compnay be allowed to build an entrance into the city on the level if some other company has already an elevated track? What the Railway Commission should do, and what Parliament should insist on, is to compel them all to come in over the same elevated tracks wherever it may be, thereby avoiding different grades; and we are trying to work that out. We are not trying to keep any railway from coming into the city of Toronto, we welcome them with open arms, but we say: Come in on reasonable terms, and if in a congested district consult the city as to the elevation of your tracks. For that reason I think the amendment already in the Bill is a good one. We have it in other Bills, and I think no injury will be done by continuing the principle and putting the same clause in Bills for other cities if they desire it.

As the Bill is in my name, perhaps a word from me may not be amiss. Unfortunately I had not read this Bill when, it was placed in my name. When the Bill came before the committee strong opposition developed, and as a citizen of Toronto I thought that opposition was perfectly justified. I asked the promoters and solicitor of the road if they were prepared to accept the standard amendments which appeared in the Toronto and Eastern Railway Company's Bill. They said, certainly they were. The matter was put to the committee, and it was so carried and so ordered. Let me touch first of all upon the complaint of the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). There is no doubt that the city of Toronto is very badly served by radial railways. That is not the fault of the Parliament of Canada, nor the fault of the
[DOT]3276

legislature. In the first place, Toronto's street railway gauge is not the standard gauge. Everybody knows that radial railway to be successful must be able to carry express and light freight, and be able to handle freight cars, but no radial railway of standard gauge can match up to the traffic of the Toronto street railway, which is carried on a different gauge.
I had the good or bad fortune to be reporting the council of the city of Toronto when that agreement was made.	They decided then that they
did not want any freight traffic over their streets, and they fixed their gauge so that the radial or steam railways could not move along their streets as they do in Winnipeg, St. Louis, Chicago and other places; so a radial coming into the city of Toronto must have a special track of its own or the gauge of some part of the street railway of Toronto must be altered. I think myself that the time has come when the city of Toronto must come to this Parliament to ask for a Bill enabling it to construct certain tracks across the city, if need be, so as to connect up with radial lines of an international character such as this, and which require a Dominion charter. Toronto is opposed to this Bill, and it has been pointed out to me that if this Bill passes in its original form it will virtually give a franchise to this company, on the level, over every street in the city of Toronto. I would prefer to sacrifice my seat in this House rather than have such an injustice done to the city of Toronto, or any other city, and I think that should be the feeling of every hon. member here If the Bill as originally drafted contains such clauses, and does not contain the necessary safeguards for the city, it would be a very great injustice to Toronto, and a very valuable charter to the people who got it. As the promoters have accepted these clauses, and have never expressed anything to me to the contrary, notwithstanding everything that has occurred in this House, I do not see why any hon. member should get up and argue in favour of putting the Bill back in its original form. Bills have been passing in this form for years, and I think all interests will be served if the Bi'l passes .in its present form. I live within gunrhot of the Canadian Pacific railway tracks in the city of Toronto and close to the railway right of way mentioned by my hon. friend, and I know that the Canadian Pacific track has [Mr. Currie. 1
been elevated for a considerable distance and in a few months will be elevated right across the centre of the city. Having seen people killed at level crossings, and having narrowly escaped, myself, once in the city of Toronto, I have no great friendship for level crossings. I think this House has made up its mind that the day of level crossings is ended so far as any new charters are concerned. If this charter is all right and the road was needed, it should have been built [DOT] a number of years ago when the promoters had all the rights which it is held they now want.. I think the committee will be perfectly justified in putting the Bill through as it is, instead of obstructing it and ending by not passing it at all. We have very few minutes left in which to pass it.

This is not a new
quarrel. I think the trouble of keeping radial railways out of Toronto commenced a good many years ago.
When I was young.

When more of us
were young, younger than the ex-Minister of Railways. The Hamilton and Toronto Radial railway was the first to be refused the right to go into the city of Toronto. It has been constructed and is running as far as the town of Oakville in my county, which is about twenty miles from Toronto. Some portions of the road between Oakville and Toronto have been completed, but no entrance has been obtained into the city of Toronto; and consequently the promoters of the road are not attempting to connect up the different links between the city of Toronto and, I think, Mimico. True, legislation was passed by this House to enable that road to go into the city of Toronto, but it was on such onerous terms that it was impossible for the promoters to finance it, and consequently the matter has been practically abandoned. It was blocked simply because the city of Toronto got support enough to make the road so terribly expensive that the promoters could not raise the money, and the result is that the road is at a standstill, and will be until some cheaper way of getting into the city is found. I think the next Bill that came before us [DOT]was that for the railway on the east side of Toronto coming from Oshawa or Whitby. The same fight was continued there. The people of Toronto, desirous of keeping every radial railway out of the city-
No, no.
They will have a chance to get Georgetown stone then.
Yes, they will get it in abundance and get good stone too.
Would-the hon. gentleman prefer to have the Bill talked out or to have it withdrawn?
The hon. gentleman cannot withdraw the Bill without the consent of the House.

My right hon. friend who now leads the Government (Mr. Borden) had a policy of his own in regard to the operation of the Intercolonial railway. The basis of that policy was the constitution of a non-partisan commission to rid the railway from all the evils of patronage and of political influence in regard to its operation and to provide for the operation of the railway solely and purely as a business proposition. My right hon. friend, I have no doubt, was sincere when he made those professions in 1907 and in various years down to the moment when the responsibility of dealing with the situation was placed upon him. Then my right hon. friend forgot the promises which he had made, the professions which he had uttered, and we have the system which exists to-day on the. Intercolonial railway. When my right hon. friend had the responsibility of action in dealing with these propositions, he forgot all these professions, and, instead of having a non-partisan commission, he proceeded to do away with the commission which he found in existence when he came to power, and to appoint, as general manager of the road the gentleman who now fills that office. Under the regime of this gentleman we have gone back to all the evils of which my right hon. friend then complained. Partisanship in regard to the employment of men on the Intercolonial exists not only to the degree which he denounced some years ago, but to a very -much greater degree than ever before in the whole history of the road. No man can be employed on the Intercolonial to-day unless he has a letter to the responsible official having to do with the operation of the road, from the Conservative member of the constituency, or from the Conservative defeated candidate, or from the Conservative committee. The Minister of Trade and .Commerce, who sits next the Prime Minister, in the last Parliament moved in this House a resolution in which he condemned in the strongest possible terms the evils of patronage as applied to the selection of officials upon mere party grounds, and as to the purchase of supplies from political friends. Why is it that to-day these professions are forgotten, not only with regard to the employment of -men, but in regard to the furnishing of -supplies to the Intercolonial railway, for no man is allowed to furnish supplies to
[The Chairman.]
that railway unless his name is on the patronage list. And when it comes to the question of the distribution of contracts, I have known the present Minister of Railways to call for tenders for important supplies, and to disregard the tenders sent -in and to proceed to distribute among his .party friends the proportion of the articles required, according as it suited his political judgment.
In regard to the question of dealing with the men, I have here a letter from an employee of the road who gives cases which indicate how, under the present management, men who get drunk while engaged in operating trains are treated with favouritism by the present officials. Here is the case of a conductor whose train while unprotected was run into iby another train, and the conductor had been taking a little something, and thirty demerits were charged against him. A railway engineer in Truro yard was taken off his engine and put on a shunter in the yard because he was shown to have been drunk; another one who had been working on a shunter was given a lower grade of employment, simply and solely because he had political influence to get the rules disregarded. There is a conductor on the Intercolonial railway running out of Truro, who is known to everybody in the province of Nova Scotia who travels on the train as having been frequently drunk while on duty. He was discharged, but he had the political influence to be taken back and he is now running as a baggage-master on one of the through trains of the Intercolonial. These are the conditions that exist to-day, and when my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. EmmeTson) moves asking the House to condemn these things, the Prime Minister should remember what he said seven years ago, and if he meant what he said he should at least take hold of this question and, as has been suggested by his own friends, he should inquire into the management of the Intercolonial and see whether he cannot fulfil some of his promises in regard to it.
