speechtext: Will my hon. friend give the names of these men to whom he has referred?
It was done long before Mr. Cochrane came into office.
The introduction of these rates was not done long before he came into office.

Yes, it was.
M)r. MACDONALD: Excuse me, it was not.
The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) had an Order in Council ready.

Whether the hon.
member for South Renfrew had an Order in Council or not, the increase of rates never took place under Liberal rule.
That is because you went out of power.

Let hon. gentlemen on both sides be judged by their actions. Who put these increased rates into force? They were put into force under the regime of the Hon. Mr. Cochrane. And for what purpose? For the purpose of extracting more and unnecessary money out of the provinces down by the sea. The hon. Minister of Railways found, after he had put these (rates into force, that there came from every portion of the country vehement objection to his action. So, when Mr. Hayes came in, he was sent around to deal with the question. And what did he do?
Reduced the rates.

Not at all. The
rates were increased in the first place from twenty-five to fifty per cent according to the schedule. In my own constituency the products of the farm and the products of the coal mines were increased from thirty to fifty per cent. But after these rates had been in force for some time along came Mr. Hayes. Did he bring these rates back to where they had been under Liberal rule? Not at all. But instead of decreasing them by from thirty to fifty per cent, he increased them anywhere from fifteen to thirty per cent. And them the acting minister tells us that he reduced them. A nice

solutely incorrect statement which he made in giving another reason for the procedure to which I have referred. He said that he did not want the sidings filled up during the winter with steamship freight eoming from Halifax. Fortunately the information extracted from hon. gentlemen opposite by the hon. member for Guys-borough shows the baseless character of that defence for this absolutely unjustifiable proceeding. In an answer obtained by the hon. member for Guysborough to a question he asked the other day, it is stated that the quantity of freight which originated in the province of Nova Scotia during the past year was 2,693,024 tons. What proportion of that amount was made up of freight which came from the seaport of Halifax? This tremendous amount of freight which prevented the general manager of the Intercolonial railway from keeping the coal mines of Nova Scotia going and from saving the coal miners from want. The proportion is 1/26-99,308 tons. That covers not merely the months of December, January, February and March, but the month of April of the previous year as well. So that the freight with which Mr. Gutelius did not want to interfere is but an infinitesimal portion of the freight going over the Intercolonial in winter. I want to submit to hon. gentlemen on the other side the question: Is it fair or right that we who live along the line of the Intercolonial railway and who are debarred in winter from connection by water with the central parts of the Dominion, should be told by the Government railway: we will not burn the coal that you produce in Nova Scotia; we will not haul it over the Government railway; we prefer to pay $1.50 more a ton to the Yankees than to buy our own coal and employ our own men on the Intercolonial railway. Is it any wonder that the hon. member for Westmorland moves a resolution asking that the operation of the railway under these conditions be condemned?
Having given that excuse as to why he purchased the coal last fall in the United States, what did the general manager do next? What did he do when the spring came, when the steamers were running to Montreal and there was no extra freight coming oveT the Intercolonial from the Atlantic coast? He shows the absolute flimsiness of his excuse by writing to the following companies:
J. Bert Ross, Buffalo, N.T.
American Steel Company, Pittsburg-, Pa.
Moreland Coke Company, Pittsburg, Pa.

Ernest Law & Company, Philadelphia, Pa.
Keystone Coal and Coke Co., Philadelphia, Pa.
Watkins Coal Company, Philadelphia, Pa.
Pennsylvania Coal and Coke Co., New York, N.Y.
Geo. Hall Coal Company, Ogdensburg, N.Y.
J. H. Weaver and Company, Philadelphia, Pa.
Whitney and Kemmerer, Philadelphia, Pa.
Widnoon Coal Mining Co., Buffalo, N.Y. t
H. W. Somers, Albany, N.Y.
He asks these coal operators in the United States if they will submit to him an offer to -supply all the coal required on the Intercolonial railway during the year 1914, 750,000 tons. When the general manager of the road, in the interview which he gave at Montreal, put forward the excuse which he did for purchasing coal from the George Hall Company last fall, he did not give the country the whole truth, If he did, why did he, in the spring of this year, ask fifteen American coal companies whether they would supply coal to the Intercolonial for this year? If somebody had not called public attention to the fact, the acting Minister of Railways and Canals would have been compelled-and I know he would have disliked it very much-to stand up in this House and admit that the Intercolonial Railway management had purchased summer -coal in the United States, and try to apologize for it.
Fortunately for him we succeeded in calling public attention to this matter and scared the general manager of the Intercolonial off so that he did not venture to award any contract for this year to the American coal people. All the while the Department was dickering with these operators in the United States, in every coal centre in Nova Scotia there were women and children who were suffering from want under the conditions that exist under this Government. The conditions in every coal mining town in eastern Nova Scotia during the past winter have never been equalled in any year since 1895, when, fortunately for Canada, the Conservative party were put out of power. They brought all this back again. These gentlemen with their splendid administration of the Intercolonial railway, do not know enough about what is going on down in the country which this railway serves, to know that the last thing they should have done was to do what no other railway company would have done, go to the United States and ask them to supply coal to the Intercolonial during this year.
What further? When they got these offers the general manager, notwithstanding the poor condition of the coal industry in Nova Scotia, proceeded to insist that he would not pay the coal managers of Nova

Scotia last year's prices and so he drove the coal managers of Nova Scotia under these conditions to accept a less price than was paid last year and the year before. That is what these gentlemen are doing in regard to the operation of the Intercolonial in respect of these things. What has occurred further? Of course the general manager, with his huge salary, will probably save enough under this method of oppression which he is adopting in dealing with the coal industry of Nova Scotia, to pay this large salary of his for two years. But is the game worth the candle? Not only are they doing that, but by the increased rates which have been maintained in regard to these products they absolutely prevent the exportation of coal from the Maritime provinces into the central portions of Canada. I think the hon. member for Westmorland, in proposing the resolution, has only put into language what is the opinion of everybody who lives along the line of this railway from a business standpoint. There has been also complete disarrangement of the very satisfactory conditions that have existed among the men. We have in every department of the Intercolonial railway the brotherhood systems that exist on every other railway in the country, and notwithstanding this as a result of these new methods that have been introduced the principle of promotion of men born and brought up on the Intercolonial railway has been absolutely stopped. Wherever a new position was created whose occupant would have to assume some responsibility nobody but a man from some other railway either in Canada or the United States would be appointed. I think we can claim, and the Premier will not venture to dispute the assertion, that the men who are on the Intercolonial railway, no matter what party appointed them within the last twenty-five or thirty years, are the	equal of
intelligence	and	capacity	of	any
other men on any other railway in Canada or in the United States. But no matter what the capacity or ability of a man may be he cannot be promoted. The principle seems to be that such a man is not fit for any job involving responsibility under this Government. The heartlessness that has been exhibited in regard to some cases there is striking. I have here a letter from a poor old man who has been on the railway for twelve years. One day he received a letter without any notice-no allegations of political partisanship about this, no suggestion of anything of that kind-but on March 23 this old man gets a letter as follows: ' Please arrange to make out form
86 for so-and-so, stopping this man from the service. Please see that this man is laid off on the night of March 31.'	A
week's notice to this man who is a car builder in the railway town of Stellar-ton; no complaint against him on the ground of politics; a quiet, simple old man doing his work. But some of these gentlemen in Moncton wakened up to the fact that he happened to be an old man. He had been on the road since January, 1905; his name is William Friel; he has been on the road almost ten years. If he were allowed to remain on until next year he would have qualified under the Provident Fund Act. Into that fund he had paid two and a half cents a day every day he had been on the railway since the Act came into force. He was set adrift almost ' in the middle of winter on a week's notice, no money was given him, not even the money he had paid in. He was told to go out and find what he could do; there was no fault except that he was getting old. I am bound to say that if the Minister of Railways were here-and in saying this I am not reflecting on the acting minister- he would have dealt with this case. Mr. Cochrane knows very well that there exist along the Intercolonial railway numerous cases of men who have grown old who might be thrown out in order to make way for younger men but who had not filled the allotted time. I understood that it was generally understood along the line of the Intercolonial railway that this winter legislation would be introduced to provide for these cases, that they would get back either the money that they had put in or participate in the fund, as they had a right to do. What I complain of is that men managing the Intercolonial railway have so little knowledge of our conditions down there that without any complaint against a man they discharge him on a week's notice, disregarding the claim which he had, if not in law at least in equity, upon the provident fund to which he had paid every day during his service on the road. Then there has been a rearrange^ ment of railway centres in order to gratify the political friends who exercise political pressure. Men who have been living at the various railway centres, who have their homes there, who have had the conditions of life there were twisted around, their runs were changed and they were sent to different places and compelled to be away from their homes at night without any reason whatever. If there had been in charge of the Intercolonial railway a

general manager who had been brought up on the road, these conditions would have been recognized. It is no wonder that the Truro Citizen says to the Prime Minister what the real position of his friends is on the Intercolonial railway and this because of the absolute failure of the management to realize existing conditions that prompt men to make these charges as they occur in the Truro Citizen. We heard the present minister talk about safety first, the desirability of safety first among the employees. I was very much amused to hear him dilate upon that because I discovered in the Truro Citizen, which is said to be the organ of the Conservative whip in this House-whether it is his organ or not he is said to own it ' and probably he cannot control the editor-the paper furnished a veritable gold mine of criticism. It has a sarcastic article saying that under this railway management there are a great number of well-paid men going up and down the line instructing the old employees. One of those special officials sent out from Moncton a week ago a carload of dynamite attached to a passenger train. Such a thing had never been heard of on the Intercolonial before. Dynamite had always been taken under special conditions, and the train crew protested against the car of dynamite being attached to the train on which there were twenty-two passengers.
That was safety last.

You can have a
great many theories about safety first and bring high-priced people from the United States to operate the people's road in this country, but the first thing the general manager should do is to find out all about the people for whom he is going to operate the road; that is, if he is going to operate it with any regard for their ideas. I do Diink it is the duty of the Government to tuink over, for a little while, this question of the indiscriminate employment of American citizens on the Intercolonial. No man should be proscribed on account of his (birth. Where you have to do with companies, you have one condition; but when the Government of this country employs aliens to perform Government work, you have a condition that is not to be found in any other country in the world. Why, says my hon. friend the acting Minister of Railways, these men have been in Canada a long time; therefore that answers the argument that we should net ercplov them.

They have been in Canada this long, that they do not want to give up their American citizenship. Certainly there has been some legislation removing the difficulties in regard to aliens. My hon. friend the member for Brandon (Mr. Aikins) perhaps can supply the common law on the subject of the employment of aliens under the Crown.
Might I ask the hon. member if the people of the United States do not employ hundreds of thousands of Canadians in the services of that country?

My hon. friend was talking to the Prime Minister about the Canadian Northern railway, and he did not catch my point. When he listens to it I am sure he will agree with me. I offer no objection to a corporation employing a man, no matter where they get him; but I do object to the Government of this country taking money out of the treasury to employ aliens upon Government work when they can get Canadians just as good as the aliens they are employing.

And when there are
thousands of unemployed in this country.

I think that point
should appeal to my hon. friend the acting Minister of Railways because he has had strong feelings upon this question. I recall the vigorous attitude he adopted in this House some three years ago, when he said that Canada's identity would be imperiled if certain things were done. One thing is certain, and that is that one department of the Government will soon be in the hands of an alien race-as they would put it-if the present policy is continued. The Intercolonial will soon be entirely under the control of the American people, who not only want to man it but who go across the line to buy United States coal in order to run it.
An adjunct.

Surely it is about
time this thing should stop. I am surprised at the Prime Minister allowing it, but I do not believe he knows what has been going on. Now that his attention has been called to it, I am sure he will stop it.
Quite sure ?

I am beginning to
lose confidence in my right hon. friend. He has good intentions, but so far I have failed to see him implement them.
Bad associates.

I think the Prime
Minister has voted in this House for a resolution that it is desirable in the interests of the Intercolonial that we should get branch lines. I am quite sure he has, but he has not been doing much at that particular job since coming into power. He found several propositions at hand which he might have accepted with .the greatest possible ease, and without the expenditure of much money. Having admitted the principle that it is desirable in the interests of the Intercolonial to have as many feeders for that line as possible, my right hon. friend has not been at all active in the pursuit of that laudable idea.
I do admire some hon. gentlemen opposite. When they want to excuse their inaction on any matter they say: The Senate will not permit us to do it. I have been waiting to hear a vigorous denunciation of the Senate from the Prime Minister, and an assertion on the part of the Government and himself of their intention to wipe ouit that nefarious institution; but he does not move on that line at all. He wants the Senate there to be blamed for all the things this Government have left undone that they ought to have done, and so that they can say when this branch lines question comes up: We could nolt take over branch lines because the Senate is there. My right hon. friend knows very well how flimsy that excuse is. When the Senate insisted upon the Government laying before Parliament all propositions for ratification, and insisted upon that principle alone, they were not doing anything so especially outrageous, or deserving of condemnation. My right hon. friend knows that to-morrow he could introduce into this House a Bill to ratify any arrangement that he made to take over branch lines for the Intercolonial. What does he mean by putting on the Order Paper a resolution providing all this money for the Canadian Northern railway. The Senate has not been asked to permit him to do anything of the kind. Of his own initiative he went out and made this agreement, brings it here to Parliament, and, if it is incorporated in an Act of Parliament, he has full rights to carry out the agreement notwithstanding anything the Senate has done. If he has not taken over branch lines for the Intercolonial, it is not on account of the Senate, but simply and solely because he does not want to do it. That is the whole proposition. If my right hon. friend addresses the
House upon this, question, and pays me the compliment of referring to anything I have said, I would like him to meet that proposition squarely, and let the House know as to whether the proposition I make is not correct. As a matter of law and of parliamentary practice, there is nothing to prevent him introducing a Bill, or any number of Bills, to take over any number of branch lines he wants along the line of the Intercolonial. It is just as well for the people of this country to realize that my right hon. friend and his party are responsible for not taking over those branch lines. Not only that, but my right hon. friend has utterly failed to supply the necessary branch lines for which funds had been provided when he came into power. I do submit to my right hon. friend that it was really unfair

he cannot justify it-that out of the .two branch lines for which my hon. friend the member for South Renfrew had provided funds in the session of 1911, he should have picked out the one in his own constituency, and absolutely disregarded the other one for which the people interested had been fighting for a long period of time. That was pretty shabby treatment, and unworthy of my right hon. friend. I am surprised that he should have permitted such a course to be taken. The eastern portion of Nova Scotia is entitled to that railway accommodation. What is the use of the Minister of Railways saying: If somebody will show me where I am going to get some money	out
of this thing, I will consider it. That is not the kind of policy that is adopted in other cases. It is the excuse put forward to strike out of the Estimates all the provisions which had been made by my hon. friend for (South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) and to disregard the contracts which had been entered into for a railway to Guysboro. That is part and parcel of the management of the Intercolonial railway and it is all included in the condemnation embodied in the resolution introduced by my hon. friend from Westmorland.
My hon. friend from Westmorland has referred to the terms upon which the Government have undertaken to haul Canadian Pacific railway trains from St. John to Halifax. I do not think that my hon. friend has quite caught the point in regard to the matter, if .he will permit me to say so. The reason why the Canadian Pacific railway axe paying the Intercolonial for hauling their trains from St. John to Moncton
Wh-at paper is that?

That is the Truro
Citizen, .a paper published in Truro and reputed to be owned by the Conservative whip m this House, who founded -it and, as it says, it speaks out in meetings once in -awhile. I might at greater length deal with the various questions that come up in regard to the -operation of the Intercolonial railway, but speaking from the standpoint of the Maritime provinces, living there, connected with the business life ' 10 p.m. of those provinces, knowing something of the men who work on the road, knowing something of the condition of these provinces, I say that at no time in my -recollection has there been such utter and complete disregard of the business interests of those provinces and the interests of the individual men who work upon the road -and the common people of the Maritime provinces. I shall unhesitatingly, and with the greatest possible pleasure, support the resolution of my hon. friend from Westmorland.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have spent two
or three hours very pleasantly listening to various disquisitions upon branch lines, aliens, the Senate, coal, and boards of management. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) had better get a little instruction from the late Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). He seems to think that the Intercolonial railway was managed by commission under the regime of that hon. gentleman. I have heard the hon. member for South Renfrew take exception in this House to the statement that the road was managed under a commission, and draw attention distinctly to the point which he had made that the road under his regime was not managed by a commission, but by a board of management. But the hon. member for Pictou, not having looked into that question very carefully, has fallen into a misapprehension in that regard. I take great pleasure in correcting him, and for the purpose of further detail in correction I would refer him to the hon. member for South Renfrew who has made it very plain to the House on various occasions.
My hon. friend from Pictou has made the allegation that the Intercolonial railway, under the management of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane), has been directed entirely by partisan considerations, not by considerations of reasonable business management. I take exception to that in the most unqualified terms, and I say that in so far as I have had a complaint-and I have had a complaint from time to time-in regard to the management of the Intercolonial railway, it has been that the railway has been managed too strictly on a business basis and not according to the basis upon which the management was founded in days gone by. I venture to say that if there is any dissatisfaction with the Intercolonial railway, it has proceeded from time to time more from the fact that the Minister of Railways and Canals has been disposed to give what has been regarded as too strict attention to purely business considerations in the management of the road. I do not think that any hon. gentleman who knows anything of the management of the Intercolonial railway during the last two or three years will venture to dissent from what I have stated in that regard.
A good deal has been said about the freight rates on the Intercolonial railway, but the hon. member for Westmorland apparently has not a very clear recollection of what took place under his own regime.
He has asserted that an Order in Council is necessary to increase freight rates on the Intercolonial; but if he remembered clearly and distinctly the facts, he would, as I am informed, have known that an Order in Council was passed fixing maximum rates on the Intercolonial according to the standard in force on the Drummond Counties railway, and this without any special Order in Council, under the management,of hon. gentlemen opposite, the rates on the Intercolonial were increased, because the increase did not bring them up to that maximum. I am also informed that the recent freight rate increases on the Intercolonial have never on any occasion reached that maximum, and that therefore no Order in Council was necessary, nor has one been passed. My hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson) does not seem to have been very well informed on this point. As to the increase in rates, the justification put forward by the Minister of Railways in this House last year, and I think by the acting minister this year, was, that certain items, amounting altogether to nearly $800,000 per annum, constituted an increase in the cost of operating the Intercolonial, and that among these items were a very proper increase of wages to the employees of the Intercolonial and a very large increase in the cost of coal, which together amounted to nearly $600,000. The Minister of Railways, acting within the maximum rates which had been fixed, not by us but by our predecessors in office, sanctioned certain increases of rates. Those increases were apparently not very well considered in respect to certain items, and complaints were made-and I am bound to say that I think those complaints in some instances were fully justified. Mr. Hayes, who had been appointed as freight traffic manager of the Intercolonial, was directed by the minister, with whom I had conference on the subject, immediately to inquire into these alleged grievances in every case, and, so far as I am informed, at present every grievance that was brought to the attention of the management of the Intercolonial railway or to the attention of the minister has been inquired into and wholly or in large measure redressed. I do not think there is in the province of Nova Scotia at the moment any very serious complaint with regard to increases of rates, upon which subject my hon. friend from Westmorland has so dilated.
He and my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) have dwelt upon the iniquity of the management of the Intercolonial railway by reason of the fact that certain persons who happen to have been born

south of the boundary line between Canada and the United States, but who had been residents and citizens of this country for a great many years, are at present in the employment of the Intercolonial railway. One would think to hear these gentlemen that there was hardly any person in the employment of the Intercolonial railway who was not an American citizen. I have no personal knowledge of the subject, but I made inquiry since this debate began, and I am informed that every .superintendent upon (the Intercolonial railway to-day is a Canadian citizen, and, with the exception of Mr. Richardson, has been brought up -and trained in the service of the Intercolonial. That does not accord very well with the picture that has been drawn by the hon. member for Westmorland and the hon. member for Pietou.
I am entirely in agreement with these gentlemen on the principle that it is a proper thing fox men who have been in the service of that railway to be promoted from time to time so far as their abilities will justify and sio far as their experience will warrant. I would want no other system than that upon the Intercolonial or upon any other railway in this country, and I believe that that principle will be carried out and is being carried out on the Intercolonial. But it is necessary from time to time to obtain some person with peculiar and special experience in a particular line of railway management; and I believe it is only in that connection that a few men, I do not know how many, have been brought in, either from the Canadian Pacific railway or from the Grand Trunk.
The hon. member for Westmorland has taken upon himself to say that there has been not only this indiscriminate dealing in aliens, as he calls them, but that the assistant superintendent is the brother-inlaw of the general superintendent. I do not know that even if that were true it would necessitate taking up more than an hour or two of the time of Parliament in dilating on it; but, as a matter of fact,
I am informed-and I sent a telegram for the purpose of inquiring about it-that there is not one word of truth in that assertion. The charge of nepotism, as it seems to be based. wholly upon the fallacious illustration which the hon. gentleman brought forward, falls completely to the ground.
There has been, I daresay, some dissatisfaction with regard to the management of the Intercolonial railway, both under

this Administration and under the late Administration; but I would like the hon. member for Pietou to remember that that dissatisfaction has not arisen solely in respect to officials appointed by the present Administration. If I am not absolutely mistaken, the hon. member for Pietou himself went on strike, if I may use a common expression, on account of his dissatisfaction with a gentleman appointed by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) when he wa.s minister, to a very important position on that railroad. I am very glad to observe that the hon. member for Pietou bows assent to what I have just said.
I did not bow.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It perhaps was an involuntary bowing of the head which might under the circumstances be taken to give assent.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There has been a great deal of time taken up in discussing the purchase of coal. One would suppose that the 14,000 tons of coal, which were purchased last year by the Intercolonial railway from the United States under very special circumstances, constitute the only case in which coal was purchased for that railway. I think some 60,000 tons were purchased about 13 years ago by the late Administration.
Mr. MA'ODONAILD: How much was it? Mr. BORDEN: 60,000 tons.
Never delivered?
Oh, yes.
Any coal that was purchased in the United States was purchased at the time of a strike.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In the first place, my hon. friend says the coal was not purchased at all, and then he says if it was purchased it was purchased during a strike. I think he is confusing two cases: one in which the hon. member for Westmorland was very anxious to have large purchases of coal made in the United States, and the other in which there were actually large purchases of coal made there.
Not in my day, as I recall it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Perhaps not in my hon. friend's day, but I will read documents that will convince him that he was very

anxious that there should be such purchases. In 1901, I think it was, there was a purchase of 60,000 tons of American coal by the late Government. My hon. friend from Pictou says that that was purchased by reason of a strike in one of the mines.
More than one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: How many?
A general strike, as I recollect it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think there was any general strike in the coal mines of Nova Scotia at that time.
In different counties.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I speak subject to correction, but I am not aware of any conditions such as my hon. friend mentions having existed at that time, and I believe that what took place was this: A certain coal company, or perhaps more than one- I am not familiar personally with the facts -was not able to fulfil its contract with the Government, and therefore the Government purchased 60,000 tons of coal in the United States. If we are to apply the argument to which we have listened, and with which we have been edified by the hon. member for Pictou, why did not the Government procure that coal from the mines where there was no strike? I presume it may have been because those mines not having made contracts for the delivery of that coal, the Government were not in a position to call upon them. And I should think that if my hon. friend had given to this .subject proper reflection, which evidently he did not give, he might have arrived at the conclusion that the same conditions brought about the purchase of the
14,000	tons of coal to which he has alluded and in contemplation of which he almost wept during the course of his speech.
The general manager never asked fifteen of the nineteen companies whether they could deliver.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Neither did they in the case to which I refer, so far as I am aware. Does the hon. gentleman undertake to say-

Better bring down
the papers about that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
thinks so, he should have fortified himself with the facts before he undertook to make this charge-*
I have all the papers in the case to which I refer. I proved what I alleged, and it cannot be controverted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend knew
perfectly well in this other case the reasons which brought it about, and he might very well have reached the conclusion that precisely similar reasons brought about the purchase of a much smaller quantity of coal during the past year.
I know what the circumstances were in that case, and I do not know about the other.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will tell my hon. friend something about the circumstances to which he has alluded and which perhaps he does not know.

Then, the papers
should have been brought down.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Dominion Coal Company had a contract for 100,000 tons of coal to be furnished from the Springhill mines. The quantity they should have delivered by the end of September at the average monthly rate was 50,000 tons; they had actually delivered 41,335 tons, or nearly 9,000 tons short. The Maritime Coal, Railway and Power Company was under contract to supply 120,000 tons. By the end of September they should have delivered 55,600; they had delivered only 49,850 tons. The Minudie Coal Company were under contract to deliver 130,000 tons; by the end of September they should have delivered 65,000 tons; they had delivered only 17,333 tons. The Acadia Coal Company were under contract to deliver 100,000 tons; they should have delivered by the end of September 50,000; they had actually delivered more than that-57,680 tons.
The Intercolonial Coal Mining Company was under contract to deliver 65,000 tons; their deliveries up to the end of September should have been 37,500 tons, but the actual deliveries were only 14,240 tons. It is only fair to observe that in the contract with the Minudie Company there is included 60,000 tons of run-of-mine coal. The company were under the impression that this tender had not been accepted, but Mr. Lavoie said it was-the' Intercolonial railway, through their officer, was under the impression that there was that contract. Under these circumstances, as the time had passed in v hich the coal could be ordered from Nova Scotia to be delivered by water carriage, 13,393 long tons were ordered from the George Hall Company at $3 net ton delivered f.o.b. cars Massena Springs; duty 53

cents, freight 57J cents, total $4.10i per net tom delivered at Ste. Rosailie Junction. Under the circumstances, I do not know what the Intercolonial railway authorities could otherwise have done. They were able to get 17,334 tons from the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company at $3.95 per gross ton delivered in vessels at Princess pier near Point Levis, and also from the Canadian Import Company, agents of the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, 15,000 tons at $4.20 per gross ton f.o.b. ears at their discharging plant, Montreal. But they were obliged to get also 14,000 tons from the United States, and they did so for the reason I have mentioned and no other. Under the circumstances, I think there is ample precedent in what took place ten or twelve years ago for the purchase made last year.
Now, as I have stated, in 1900 or 1901,
60,000	tons of American coal were purchased by the late Government. This was not because there was a strike, as the statement was given to me, but because a strike among the miners in Nova Scotia was anticipated, and this quantity of American coal was laid in to prevent the railway being caught short. This coal cost $4.85 per gross ton. At that time the railway was not paying custom charges, but duty has been included to make the comparison. The hon. member for Westmorland, I am informed, was very anxious in 1907 to have extensive purchases of coal from the United States. To refresh his memory, I will read one or two telegrams furnished me by the Department of Railways and Canals, which would seem to indicate that what I have said is quite correct.

There was a great
strike in that year, and the Dominion Coal Company, the biggest producers in the province, were not raising coal at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend nods his head as if he thought he had scored a great point, but I would like to say to him that I think Mr. Butler succeeded in making arrangements to get the coal elsewhere. Here is a telegram-
Cleveland, Ohio, Nov. 13, 1907.
M. J. Butler,
Deputy Minister of Railways,
Ottawa, Ont.
If coal not secured, could make good arrangements here Pittsburg run-of-mine, which would satisfactorily meet your requirements. Could you inform through rate gross ton from Cheswiek on Bessemer and Lake Brie railway via International Bridge and Grand Trunk to Montreal or Ste. Rosalie? Wire early to-morrow Hollonden House here.
H. R. Emmerson.
Here is another from Mr. Butler:
Ottawa, Ont., Nov. 14, 1907. Hon. H. R. Emmerson,
Hollanden House,
Cleveland, Ohio.
Please make best price f.o.b cars. We will figure out duty and freight and will take care of same for say 50,000 tons.
M. J. Butler.
The hon. member for Westmorland then sent this telegram:
Cleveland, Ohio, Nov. 14, 1907.
M. J. Butler,
Deputy Minister of Railways,
Ottawa, Ont.
Can arrange 50,000 tons delivered on cars Cheswiek, Pennsylvania, at rate of one thirty-eight two thousand pounds. Delivery beginning first of December, finished first March. Wire me Manhattan hotel, New York, to-morrow, if you wish me act. Coal represented very best for your purposes. Could get cheaper quality. Would require special arrangement made for return of cars to International Bridge to prevent detention by Grand Trunk.
H. R. Emmerson.

I was not Minister of Railways at that time; I was simply getting some information for Mr. Butler. The statement referred to the period when I was Minister of Railways, and I stated that there was no actual purchasing during that period. This relates to a later period, when the hon. member for South Renfrew was Minister of Railways. If I had been minister, it is well recognized that my views on fiscal matters as a free trader would have justified the action.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Let me read another telegram from Mr. Butler:
Ottawa, Ont., Nov. 15, 1907. Hon. H. R. Emmerson,
Manhattan Hotel,
New York, U.S.A.
Have placed order with Moreland Company for twenty thousand tons at lower price and hope to get balance of requirements from Nova Scotia.
M. J. Butler.
I was simply getting some information for Mr. Butler.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Apparently, as Minister of Railways my hon. friend thought that this coal should be purchased outside of Canada, but as a private citizen he thinks it is right to buy it in the United States. That is a rather remarkable suggestion.
Coming back for a moment to the rates which I mentioned a moment ago, I am informed by officials of the Department of Railways and Canals that although there has been this slight increase in rates upon the Intercolonial, they are lower to-day than corresponding rates on the Canadian Pacifie railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific

railway, the Canadian Northern railway and the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway. Of course, I have no personal knowledge of that, nor, indeed, would I be competent to make a comparison of the rates, but that is the information which has been afforded by the officials of the department.
The hon. member for Westmorland endeavoured to make a very strong case against the Government in connection with an arrangement which was negotiated between Mr. Gutelius and Mr. Boswell of the Canadian Pacific railway, and my hon. friend is of the opinion that the rates are altogether too low. Is my hon. friend aware of the fact that under his own administration, in the case of wheat carried from points in Ontario to Halifax, for the 837 miles of haulage over the Intercolonial railway, the Intercolonial received only 95 cents per ton? The hon. member will see that as the distance from Halifax to St. John is a little less than one-third of the distance from Halifax to Montreal, the corresponding rate in respect of the distance from Halifax to Montreal would be $1.85 per ton. The comparison so far as flour is concerned is perhaps not so cogent. Flour from Toronto is carried to Halifax over the Intercolonial railway, and the share of the Intercolonial railway for the 837 miles of haulage from Stontreal to Halifax is $1.49. Under the arrangement which has been made between the Canadian Pacific railway and the Intercolonial railway, the corresponding rate would be about $1.85. I do not pretend to have sufficient knowledge to say whether or not this is a fair rate, and with all due deference to my hon. friend the member for Westmorland, although he was for a certain period Minister of Railways and Canals, I doubt very much whether he has the expert knowledge to make the necessary comparisons and to take into consideration everything which must be taken into account in coming to a conclusion as to whether or not this is a paying rate. Officials of the Intercolonial railway who have this matter in hand say that the rate is a paying rate under the circumstances, and a fair rate. In the absence of anything better than has been suggested here to-night, I am bound to accept their conclusion, and so is the Minister of Railways and Canals. Further than that, I placed before this House on a previous occasion a comparison of this rate with rates upon grain which was hauled in 1903 and 1904 from Parry Sound to Halifax. I pointed out then in detail what I shall
only allude to at the present time, that is to say, that the rate provided in the contract between Mr. Gutelius and Mr. Boswell is very much higher than the rate which the late Administration said was a fair and paying rate at that time-two or three times as high, if I remember correctly. The statement is already upon ' Hansard,' and I shall not take up the time of the House in giving it again.

I do not pose as a
freight rate expert, but I was pointing out from, the return of the Department of Railways that it was costing the Intercolonial much more for train hauling between St. John and Halifax than they were getting. I was not presuming or assuming; I was making and basing my assertions upon the figures furnished by the department itself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend did not
take into account some of the things which are contained in the agreement: the assumption of clerical work, checking, waybilling and accounting, by the Canadian Pacific railway, and, so far as I understand, the assumption by the Canadian Pacific railway of certain liability for loss and damage, as well as of certain terminal charges. There are a great many matters of that kind which must necessarily be taken into account. It, is necessary also to take into account, as I understand it, the rate at which new and additional business may be profitably carried when the road is already under operation.
I am informed by the traffic expert of the Intercolonial railway that, taking all these things into consideration, the rate provided in the agreement which has been alluded to was a fair and reasonable rate.
My hon. friend has endeavoured to cast discredit upon the statements made in this House as to the surplus claimed for the operation of the Intercolonial railway last year. I understand that $300,000, or $25,000 per month, was set aside for the improvement of equipment, and that $300,000 was set aside at the end of the year for the same purpose, making a total of $600,000 taken out of the income of the road for the purpose of improving equipment and keeping it up to the proper standard. My hon. friend has endeavoured to cast discredit on that by comparing the railway statistics issued by the department but made up for a different fiscal year; they are made up for the year ending 30th of June, while the accounts of the Intercolonial railway are kept by the ordinary

fiscal year of the Government, which ends 31st of March. I do not think that any comparison instituted in that way could be a very fair or convenient comparison, and the statements given to the House by the acting minister in that respect are statements furnished to him by his officials on which he has a right to rely and upon which also the House has a right to rely in the absence of some criticism more cogent than that which the hon. member for Westmorland has been able to make against it.
He also finds fault with the standard rules. I do not know very much about these rules. I do not know in what respect they differ from the rules which have prevailed in the past on certain portions of the Intercolonial railway but the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada has made it necessary for all railways of Canada subject to its jurisdiction to adopt these rules. My hon. friend from Westmorland says that these rules constitute a menace not only to the men employed on the Intercolonial railway hut to the passengers carried on that road, at least I so understood him. It seems to me remarkable that rules adopted by all the great railways of Canada, except the Intercolonial railway, and approved by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada are likely to constitute a menace to the men employed on the Intercolonial railway or to the people carried over it. My hon. friend from Westmorland-

My right hon. friend did not quite apprehend my statement. My complaint was that they were making the change so suddenly when other railways have taken two or three years to bring about the change gradually, not attempting to do it within so short a period, and that in doing so it was a menace and a danger to the railway and to the passenger.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend would have more knowledge as to matters of that kind than I would as he has been in charge of the Railway Department; but, with deference to what he has. said, my information is that roads have sometimes adopted these rules within a shorter period than that provided in the case of the Intercolonial railway. Certainly there is no desire to *act oppressively towards these men or to have the rules 'adopted in too short a time. I am not aware of the terms on which these rules are to Ibe adopted, hut I am sure that the time provided is ample and I cannot understand what motive could

induce those who' are managing the Intercolonial railway to seek to adopt these rules within too short a period. If there is any error in that respect it is an error of judgment and not of intention most assuredly, and I Still deny that there is any such danger as my hon. friend suggests.
Returning to the question of promotion upon the Intercolonial, as I said, I am heartily in sympathy with the idea of men working up in the service as their experience 'and ability will entitle them to work up and I know that the Minister of Railways and Canals has that idea in mind also, and wishes to carry it out. He wishes to carry it out apart from any party political consideration. I know that that is his thought; but as a matter of fact for many years now past we have had this experience upon the Intercolonial railway. We found men leaving the Intercolonial railway and going into the service of other railways, either in Canada or the United States, and obtaining very high positions. I remember Mr. Pottinger, whose management of the Intercolonial has been referred to in terms of praise to-night-and in those terms I entirely concur-I remember that within the last 'two years. Mr. Pottinger made out for me a 'memorandum of twelve or fifteen men who had entered railway service on the Intercolonial railway during the period when he was general manager, who had left the service under one Government or the other and had attained splendid positions in the United States or in Canada. That does sometimes happen, and I for one am very sorry that the Intercolonial should lose such men. I would like to have the services of these men retained for the Intercolonial railway and I hope and, more than that, I am absolutely confident that the Minister of Railways and Canals will adopt no other policy or principle in his management of the Intercolonial of Canada. It is a right principle, it is a proper principle that there 'should be promotion according to ability and experience and that men who have the capacity to hold high positions in the service of any railway, should iu the service of the Intercolonial be promoted as their ability and their experience would justify. If any departure from a policy of that kind should be entered upon, as far as the Intercolonial railway is concerned, I for one would be disposed to enter my strongest caveat against it, because the principle which 'has been spoken of in that regard by the hon. member for Westmorland and the hon. mem-

her for Pi-ctou is an absolutely sound and correct principle in which I thoroughly concur.
Something has been said about branch lines, and if I am not mistaken my hon. friend the member for Pictou has challenged me to make some observations upon this question. Otherwise I would not refer to it as my views with regard to it have been expressed on more than one occasion. The hon. member for Pictou says that if at any time we desire to acquire a branch line for the Intercolonial railway in any part of the country upon any terms whatever, we can do it, we can come in here and be absolutely sure that the proposal of the Government will receive the sanction not only of this House but of the Senate. I am very glad to have the assurance of the hon. member for Pictou in that regard although it goes a little farther than I would really desire because I would hardly expect that a proposal of any kind that we might bring in here for the acquisition of a branch line of railway in any part of Canada would necessarily receive the support of one or other branch of the legislature. What happened last year is well understood, although the hon. member for Westmorland sought to minimize it. I did declare in the election of 1911 that I was in favour of a general policy of acquiring branch lines for the Intercolonial, and for very good reasons as it seemed to me, because a great trunk line must necessarily have feeders and even if those feeders are not profitable at the very first they usually become profitable in a very few years. A road cannot exist without local traffic, and local traffic can only be gathered up in a large way by means of these feeders. We brought in last session a Bill in the form of a resolution empowering the Minister of Railways and Canals to make contracts for the purchase or sale of branch lines, and it was in terms so wide that when I discussed the subject with the Minister of Railways after it had been debated in committee I frankly told him that I thought his resolution was too wide and conferred too much power upon him, and I myself drafted a resolution in very much narrower terms which I brought into the House, handed to my hon. friends opposite and asked them if they desired to take time to consider it. They looked over it and said that they did not desire delay and that they thoroughly approved of it. It passed the House unanimously and the Minister of Railways and Canals introduced the Bill. The hon. member for Westmorland had criticised the first resolution 208
but he did not criticise the second. When the Bill was introduced he raised the question as to whether or not the lines which the minister might construct, should exceed ten miles in length. We were prepared to cut the figures down from twenty-five to twenty miles, but the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) entered a strong protest against it being cut down at all. My hon. friend from Westmorland did not seem to have any support, so it went through in that way. It went to the Senate, and some hon. gentlemen opposite have stated in the course of this debate that the Bill came back from the Senate in a workable form. I say it came back from the Senate meaning absolutely nothing. It simply said that we could do what every hon. gentleman on the opposite -side of the House has said we can do without any Bill. It provided that the Minister of Railways might make a contract and bring it to Parliament for ratification; but he can do that, as has been urged by hon. gentlemen opposite, without any Bill. Therefore, the Bill as amended by the Senate meant absolutely nothing, because it conferred no greater powers on the Minister of Railways than those which, according to the statements of hon. gentlemen opposite, he possesses at the present time. I expected that the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who had unanimously concurred in this Bill would stand strongly in support of the Bill which had passed this House without one dissenting voice, and therefore, with some confidence I rose in my place and said: 'We cannot agree to the amendments of the Senate, because they have absolutely emasculated the Bill and made it meaningless and useless.' To my astonishment the very gentlemen on the other side of the House who had concurred in the terms of the resolution which I had drafted as embodied in the Bill, stood up and voted that they were absolutely wrong on the previous occasion. Now, this story is not out of comic opera; it is a sober and accurate statement of what actually took place in this Parliament last session.

The resolution as orginally proposed was then withdrawn, and Mr. Cochrane substituted therefor the resolution which I had submitted to my right hon. friend. That resolution went through the committee without a dissenting voice, and the Bill founded upon it went through this House without a dissenting voice, and when the amendments came back from the Senate-unless I am very much mistaken-hon. gentlemen opposite stood up and voted in support of those amendments.

I do not think that

I will not contradict my hon. friend in that regard, because I have not a clear recollection, but at all events that is the history of what took place on that occasion. So far as branch lines are concerned, we are absolutely of the same opinion as we have always been. We think that a number of branch lines ought to be acquired if they can be purchased or leased on reasonable terms. We are desirous of going on with that policy, and hope to carry it out in one way or another in the early future.
So far as the general condition of the Intercolonial is concerned, I am sure that the description which my hon. friend has given of the service upon that road is one which he can hardly be prepared to endorse upon a little reflection. He said that the passenger service and the freight service have deteriorated; that the roadbed has not been kept up to the proper standard. For my part, I have had no knowledge or intimation that such is the case except that

which I have derived from my hon friend the member for Westmorland. I know it is the desire of the Minister of Eailways and Canals to keep that road up to the highest possible .standard, and to give the best possible service to the people of Canada, especially the people of Quebec and the Maritime provinces. My hon. friend from Westmorland and other members of this House will- remember that the efforts of the Minister of Eailways and Canals in that regard have received marked and unusual commendation from some of their own political friends in the Maritime provinces.
I am sorry that some [reflections have been made on the Minister of Eailways and Canals while he is not here in person to answer them. I find no fault with any criticism of him or of his administration, because, although he is necessarily .absent, members of this House have a perfect right to criticise him as a member of the Government. I am sure, however, that notwithstanding any such criticism, hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House ais well as hon. gentlemen on this side realize that it is the desire and purpose of the Minister of Eailways and Canals to make the Intercolonial railway worthy of the people of Canada, and by means of that railway to give the best possible service to the people of this country.
Hon. GEOEGE P. GEAHAM: The right hon. the Prime Minister has invited me into this discussion. Being somewhat polite I do not like to decline the invitation. I had not intended taking any part in this discussion, as I thought the members from the Maritime provinces were fully competent to discuss the Intercolonial railway in all its phases. My right hon. friend, a moment ago, took exception to my statement that he was editing some of the proceedings of the House. I meant by that, that he was rather revising the record and putting it in a way which was not warranted by the Tecord itself. He intimated that we were performing an act of comic opera in that members of the House stood up and said they were all wrong in their previous attitude on the resolution in regard to branch lines. The Prime Minister was wrong himself, in my judgment. I think there was no vote taken in that case. There very seldom is in such a case, unless it is forced to a vote, hut the Government would not acquiesce in the amendments by the Senate.

Even if there had been a vote my hon. friend would hardly be justified. Bill after Bill comes back from the Senate amended, and these amendments are agreed to by this House, although the House has unanimously passed another kind of Bill altogether. Cases identical to the one referred to by my right hon. friend occur here every day and no person is accused of any inconsistency. We take the Bill with its amendments sooner than have no Bill at all. If that change had been adopted it would have meant that this House is in favour of branch lines with this amendment while the other side declared itself unfavourable to a Branch Line Bill, unless it could have its own scheme. My right hon. friend supported the amendment to the Bank Act, altering the Bank Act materially, and I would not charge that in voting that way he resembled comic opera because the Bank Act did not go through as he voted it should go through. These things occur every day, and there is no criticism to be directed at either side of the House or any member in it for saying: We will accept the amendment of the Senate. We do it every day, that is if a Bill is amended we accept it sooner than have no Bill at all. In the history which my hon. friend gave of the Branch Lines Bill his reference except this departure from the record was absolutely correct. In the first place, his Minister of Railways introduced a resolution that he himself said was a bad resolution I am not speaking from .comic opera; it actually occurred. His own Minister of Railways, after full consideration, no doubt, in Council brought in a Bill which was all wrong and which he could not agree to himself. I am not quoting from comic opera; I am quoting from what the Prime Minister told us. This resolution as brought in by the Government, would have allowed the Minister of Railways and Canals to have taken over the Canadian Pacific railway without coming to this House, and after a good deal of argument the Prime Minister was convinced that the resolution should be withdrawn, and he prepared another one himself. He submitted the one which he had prepared to myself, my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) and others. After conferring with my right hon. friend I said: These are powers never before given to a minister, but I am prepared to go that far so that there may be no obstacle in the way of this Government implementing the promise of its leader and taking over the 208J
branch lines. Under the Bill founded on that resolution we gave greater powers than were ever given to any minister.
Never before given.

Never given to any minister. The Senate said we went too far, and when the Bill came back with an amendment that the Government should be responsible to Parliament and that the business should not be done by Order in Council, we said: We will take the Bill as it has been amended, but hon. gentlemen opposite said: We will have the Bill passed or nothing. At bottom I do not believe the Minister of Railways wants to take over the branch lines. When I first brought in a Bill for the acquisition of branch lines, I was met with constant and persistent opposition, not by the then leader of the Opposition, but by men sitting behind him from the province of Ontario. My right hon. friend did not help me to get this Bill through at all, but it was clipped in all its features at the demand of members of the then Opposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Was it not the Senate, that clipped it?
No, the Senate did not', do the clipping at that time. It was the members behind my right hon. friend who did the clipping.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am speaking seriously; did not the Bill come back from the Senate-with a very important amendment, and were not some amendments accepted?

That was another Bill. I am referring to the first Bill that I introduced. I think that my hon. friend has reference to the second Bill that I introduced. I accepted amendment after amendment made by hon. members of the then Opposition. One of them was that no road should be taken over unless it was in the interests of the Intercolonial railway, which was a departure
11 p.m. from the idea in my mind. I accepted a number of amendments in order to get the Bill through. The then leader of the Opposition put this question to me: Does my hon. friend mean to say that he has not power now to take over branch lines if he so desires without this Bill? My reply was that the Government did have that power with the sanction of Parliament, but that I was very anxious to get the Parliament of Canada committed to the principle of taking over branch lines, and I was therefore willing

and each month there was set aside a certain sum of money for this rail renewal account. Then there were certain losses every year by the burning of freight sheds, and necessary replacements on account of small fires, and there was set aside a certain amount each year for fire protection work. That was the custom when I was in the department and I think it is the custom still, and these amounts are recognized as part of the expenditure of the Intercolonial railway, and until they are set aside each year there cannot he any surplus. I believe this is being carried out at the present time. I suppose it is the same now as it was then. And I say fearlessly, and after having investigated the matter thoroughly-for the hon. member for North Toronto and I had several tilts over this question,-that when I left the department, the Intercolonial railway was spending more money out of revenue for betterments-more by thousands of dollars - than the Interstate Commerce Commission would allow a company under their jurisdiction to spend without charging it to capital.
Out of income?

I say that the Intercolonial railway at that time spent thousands every year out of income and for betterments that the Interstate Commerce Commission would compel any company under their jurisdiction to spend on capital account. This they would do in order to protect the shareholders. It would be saying to the railway in effect: You owe that money to your shareholders in dividends and not in betterments. There is a distinct line of demarcation drawn between capital expenditures and revenue expenditures, and the Intercolonial railway, so far as my knowledge goes, exceeds the limit of what is ordinarily spent out of revenue. I think it is better that it should be in that condition than the other way.
Now, I have one word to say about branch lines in connection with the Intercolonial railway. I wish to make it clear, and I think that in what I say, I voice the opinion of practically every man in Ontario. We want the Intercolonial railway line kept up to a high state of efficiency and we want it to serve the people well, and we do not want a cent of profit ourt of it. We are prepared to bear our share of the expenditure to acquire branch lines,, not merely where they can pay but where the people require these transportation facilities wherever it will help to make these people
