more contented we are prepared to pay our share of taxation to give them such facilities as we enjoy, whether it pays the Intercolonial railway or not.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) has asked this House to say that the Government is deserving of censure in connection with the management of the Intercolonial railway for two reasons-first, because the methods of the present management are oppressive and unfair to employees and the public; and second, because the methods of the present management are detrimental to the interests of the country and of the railway. I have listened to every word of the speech of my hon. friend, as well as to every word of the speech of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and of the speech of the hon. member for South Eenfrew (Mr. Graham), and while it may be said that I am not an unprejudiced judge as to what the hon. gentleman said, yet I submit in all candor and fairness to this House, that the hon. gentlemen have not laid before the House facts that would make out a case in support of the position taken in the resolution.	*
Now, the hon. member for Westmorland dealt very largely in generalities. But where he came down, as he did in one or two instances, to give concrete examples in support of his position, it became clearly evident that he has been willing to listen to every rumour, to every word of gossip [DOT]circulated regarding the officials of the Intercolonial railway and has not taken the pains to investigate for himself, an investigation which I think the gravity of the subject would deserve, and which he should have taken before asking that the Government be censured for the acts of these officials. Early in his remarks he told the House-I think I quote him correctly- that nepotism was rampant in the affairs of the Intercolonial railway. The only instance he gave of 1 nepotism ' was that Mr. Brady had appointed a gentleman named Eichardson, who was his brother-in-law, to take the place of Mr. Hallisey, a trusted official of the Intercolonial railway. It appears now from the statement made by the Prime Minister that there was no justification for the allegation-that Mr. Eichardson is neither the brother-inlaw nor any other relation of Mr. Brady, and that he is only temporarily taking Mr. Hallisey's place, and that as soon as Mr. Hallisey recovers from the illness from

which he is suffering, which we hope will be in a very short time, he will return to the position which he has filled so long and so acceptably, and Mr. Richardson will cease to fill that position.
In his opening remarks, the hon. member referred to the branch line policy of the Intercolonial railway. In the Maritime provinces, and among those who have studied the question whether they live in the Maritime provinces or not, there is a practical consensus of opinion in favour of the Government of Canada purchasing or acquiring by some means the branch lines of railways and running them as part of the Intercolonial Railway system. The belief is that not only would such a policy be much to the advantage of the country through which these branch lines run, but in the interest of the Intercolonial railway itself, giving it important feeders. And these branch' lines operated from the head office, it is believed, would be operated more in the public interest and with greater economy than it is possible to manage them as separate unit3 each under its own company and having no harmonious management in the interest of all. Therefore this feeling strongly exists, and the hon. gentleman knowing that it exists, takes the opportunity to try to create feeling against the administration of the Railway Department by complaining that steps have not been taken for the acquisition of these branch lines. Now, I am not resorting to the tu quoque argument, but it would be interesting to ask what the hon. gentleman did to acquire branch lines when he was Minister of Railways and a supporter of the Government of the day. I think I am correct in saying that the hon. gentleman became a member of Parliament in 1900. Subsequently he became Minister of Railways. As he has been fourteen years a member of the House, and for a part of that time Minister of Railways, I think I am justified in asking what he did when supporting the Government in power or when he was himself a member of that Government to bring about the acquisition of branch lines which he condemns the Minister of Railways for not acquiring. It is true, he acquired the Canada Eastern from Fredericton to Chatham and Loggieville, a distance of about 112 miles for $300,000, or about $7,000 a mile.
It i3 136 miles.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That it is expedient to provide that the Minister of Railways may, subject to the authority of the Governor in Council, construct, purchase, lease, or otherwise acquire, in whole or in part any railway, railway bridge, railway station, railway terminal, railway ferry, or other railway work, and that any such railway or other work shall become part of the Government railway system.
That resolution was discussed at some length. Permit me to say in passing that I think my hon. friend, as well as other hon. gentlemen on the other side, did the Minister of Railways and Canals an injustice-unintentionally, no doubt-when they made the assertion that the minister was opposed to the acquisition of these branch lines. When this resolution was introduced, the hon. member for Westmorland said:
I do not think that my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane), in this instance is frank with the country in regard to it.
The following discussion then took place:
Mr. Borden: He is decidedly frank.
Mr. Emmerson: He may be frank, hut not candid. He has, in remarks which he has uttered in this House, given us to understand that he does not want to acquire any branch lines that he does not think it in the interest of the Intercolonial that they should be so acquired.
Mr. Cochrane:	I do not think I was as
frank as that.
Mr. Emmerson: Well, I so understood my hon. friend. Does my hon. friend repudiate that insinuation?
Mr. Cochrane: I repudiate the broad statement that was made. I said that I did not want to acquire some of the branch lines.
Mr. Emmerson: Well then, my hon. friend wants to acquire some of them ?
Mr. Cochrane: Yes.
This extract which I have read from ' Hansard ' shows that the contention of my hon. friend the member for Westmorland and other hon. gentlemen, who say that the Minister of Railways and Canals was opposed to acquiring branch lines, is unjustifiable. After a considerable discussion the resolution as introduced by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals was withdrawn and another substituted in its place. This resolution, which may be found on page 8874 of ' Hansard ' of the year 1913, met with the unanimous approval of the members of this House. There was no division; not a single member criticised the resolution	in any way	whatever.On May 12 the Minister of Railways and Canals moved in the House the second reading of the Bill to amend the Railway Act, and the House went into committee	thereon.	This	Bill was
criticised a little on the ground that the Government should not be allowed to build 25 miles of railway under the provisions of

this Act without first coming to Parliament for authority to do so. The contention was made that it should be reduced to 20 miles, and at that point the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) interposed in the following emphatic language :
This idea of 25 miles strikes jne with great significance, and I would not like to see it cut down at all. It fits in splendidly for the county of Victoria. I had an idea that the minister had that section particularly in his mind.
After this remark on the part of the hon. member for North Cape Breton, all opposition vanished, and the Bill was agreed to without a dissenting voice, and was sent to the Senate for consideration. Although unanimously agreed to in this House, when the Bill went to the Senate it was emasculated and its purposes entirely destroyed. Under the Bill as it came back from the Senate, no power was given to the Government other than they would possess without the passage of the Bill at all. When the Bill came back to the House the Minister of Railways moved that the Senate amendment should not be concurred in, giving the reasons therefor. A discussion ensued, and I would commend to hon. gentlemen who say that the amendment made by the Senate was harmless and that it did not affect the Bill in any way, the remarks- of the hon. member for the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley), who discussed the matter on that occasion. By his remarks he showed that he regarded the amendments made by the Senate as being very important and as very considerably affecting the Bill. He said:
It seems to me that there is not very much in issue. The amendment, as I understand it, is that such lease or contract of purchase shall be laid before Parliament for ratification. The Senate has omitted one of the most important features of the Bill; that is, the entering into a contract to build 25 miles of new road.
There we have the hon. member for the city of St. John saying that the Senate has omitted one of the most important features contained in the Bill. He goes on to suggest that there should be a conference between the House and the Senate with a view to coming to a compromise. He said:
The minister might he authorized to lease a feeder of the Intercolonial without the authority of Parliament. That is, if in any case, the minister might think it in the public interest to acquire the absolute right to the railway, he might put in the lease a provision that the minister, with the approval of Parliament, might purchase the road at a price which should be named in the lease, within a certain period of time which would be specified.

The hon. member for the city of St. John takes distinct issue with the statements made here to-night by hon. gentlemen to the effect that the amendments made by the Senate were colourless and [DOT] did not affect the Bill. He points out that they omitted one of the most important features of the Bill, and suggests a compromise in order that some arrangement should be effected.
What was the answer of the Prime Minister to that suggestion?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Prime Minister said:
Mr. Borden: I think it would be necessary to send an answer to the Senate, and I doubt very much Whether a formal conference could be held at this stage of the session, which would accomplish any good result. I think the Minister of Railways would be perfectly willing to hold an informal conference, which would answer the purpose, and some hon. gentlemen of the Senate might be appointed.
Mr. Graham: That could be done informally to-night.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier: The matter can stand. Mr. Cochrane: If you want a conference, should not the motion pass so that the Bill may go back to the Senate, and if they want a conference, I would be very glad to meet them.
In that discussion the Prime Minister stated the facts accurately as he has stated them to the House to-night, that he drafted this resolution which was substituted for the one originally introduced, that he sent it over to the member for St. John and the member for South Eenfrew, that he discussed it with them, that it was unanimously accepted by them, and that amendment went through-
-without a single word of objection and with the absolute assent of hon. gentlemen on the other side, after I had privately discussed it with the hon. gentlemen whom I have mentioned and others, and when some question was raised about reducing the twenty-five miles to twenty, the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), insisted that it should remain exactly as it was, because he hoped to havte a branch constructed in his own county.
In that the member for St. John and the member for South Eenfrew agreed, and their words are on * Hansard,' that that is an accurate account of what took place. During the debate I asked the hon. member for Westmorland if he did not say he did not think the Bill went far enough. The hon. gentleman stated that he did not recollect that he said anything of the sort. My question was based on my recollection of these words, which I find in the speech of the hon. member for Westmorland on June 5, referring to the fact
that he was anxious for the legislation to go through:
I was equally anxious because I have to acknowledge that I have taken a very deep and sincere interest in this policy. I would like to see it carried out and I would even give great powers to the Minister of Railways in respect! to the matter. I do not know but that I would go so far as to permit him to legislate on the matter, although I do not think his sympathies are quite as strong on behalf of the policy as I would like them to be. I think he has doubts and I do not think that he recognizes the branch lines as feeders, because he said on the floor of this House that they are milkers and not feeders. I certainly think it would be very desirable that an understanding should be had with the Senate. We must all be desirous of seeing this policy put into execution and of seeing these lines acquired. I do not think there is such a case of urgency with respect to the construction of branch lines because parliament is sitting long enough to enable any legislation to be put through to construct the railways. I would strongly urge that there be a conference and that some united action be taken in regard to the matter..
He also advocated giving the Ministex the power of expropriating the branch lines. What was the purpose of my hon. friend in urging that there should be a conference and that some united action should be taken in the matter, if his opinion then was as he expressed it to-night, that the Senate had not interfered with this Bill and that the Senate amendments were of a harmless character? It is perfectly clear that the gentlemen interested in the passage of this Bill, the hon. member for Westmorland and the hon. member for St. John, fully agreed with the position taken by the Minister of Eailways and the Prime Minister that the amendments made by the Senate were not only vexatious but were absolutely striking at the foundation of the Bill, and that they did not take the view put forward in this House to-night that the amendments were simple and innocent in their character and that the Bill as it came from the Senate was all that the Government would require. I desire the fact to go out to this country that it was the interference with this Bill by the friends of hon. gentlemen opposite in the Senate of this country that has prevented the Government up to the present time from taking effective measures to acquire branch line railways, and that if it had not been for the emasculation of that Bill in the Senate arrangements would have been made by which branch lines of the Intercolonial railway would have been taken over and acquired by the Intercolonial, not only in the province of New Brunswick but in every other province

through which the Intercolonial railway runs.
My hon. friend, as an instance of the way in which public interests are being neglected under the present Intercolonial management, referred to the Ocean Limited. The facts in connection with the Ocean Limited are these, that until 1913 this train never ran during the months of February and March. In 1913 the Minister of Railways and Canals made the experiment of running the Ocean Limited during those months, and the result of that experiment was a loss to this country of several hundred thousand dollars, and it was demonstrated that running the train during those months, when the travel was light and there was no tourist traffic, was not in the fiscal interest or other interest of the country. Consequently, in 1914, the Railway Department very properly as I submit, returned to the policy off not running the Ocean Limited during February and March. Why should they run that train during February and March when their experiment in 1913, when there was more railway traffic generally and more travel in the country than in 1914, had demonstrated that it could only be run at a tremendous loss to the Canadian taxpayer? It seems to me that instead of being condemned for not running the Ocean Limited during February and March in 1914, the Minister of Railways and the Railway Department, in view of their experiment in 1913, would have deserved condemnation if they had continued to run the Ocean Limited during February and March, 1914. No interest has suffered by their not doing so, and no condemnation will be made in this country of the Railway Department for their course in that respect, when the facts are known and the case is fairly placed before the people for consideration.
My hon. friend also says that there has been an increase in freight rates on the Intercolonial, and that there has been dissatisfaction in consequence. I am not prepared to dispute that statement, but a little glimpse into the past history of the Intercolonial railway will show that there has been dissatisfaction during every period of transition in regard to the management of that railway. Gentlemen within the sound of my voice to-night will remember that previous to 1896 the management of the Intercolonial railway was a frequent subject of attack, and that after the Liberal party came into power in that year and Mr. Blair became Minister of Railways the 
statement was heralded all over this country that business methods were going to prevail in the management of that road, that there would be an entire change in the system of management resulting in large surpluses and better results generally. After the Liberals had been in power for a short time they started upon this system of business management, and they pushed to one side Mr. Pottinger, who had been so long general manager. Mr. Blair sent down to manage that road a gentleman by the name of Harris then, and now, occupying a position of importance with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. What was the result? The rates were put up far higher than the ratio of increase which occurred after the change of Government in 1911. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) quoted from a newspaper published in the town of Truro to the effect that the Governmen were in danger of losing all their seats in the counties through which the Intercolonial runs. There may be gentlemen opposite -who will remember that after Mr. Harris had been in charge of the Intercolonial, and after the Government had started on their plan of business management of that road, a gentleman who represented the constituency now represented by my hon. friend from Guysborough, and who was afterwards Lieutenant-Governor of Nova Scotia, came back to this Parliament and made the announcement that if that management continued on the Intercolonial the Government would not carry a seat within fifty miles of that road. In any period of transition there is bound to be trouble. There are always people who will feel aggrieved when changes take place from any one system to any other; and therefore with the changes that have taken place in regard to the Intercolonial in recent years, with the appointing of a general manager instead of a board of control, it is not at all extraordinary that there should have been grievances among the patrons of the road in different parts of the Maritime provinces, who were not at all favourable to the changes that took place. The rate increases took place possibly without the consideration required, but I am here prepared to state that those increases made under the Order in Council passed by the previous Government-not by this Government- were small compared with the rate increases made by the Liberal Government after they came into power in 1896. A gentleman of prominence in the commercial life of St.

John-a largo patron of the Intercolonial, and one whose word would carry weight wherever he is known, and that is very generally throughout this country-made an estimate showing that in consequence of the readjustment made when the Liberals came into power in 1896, an additional $100,000 were taken from the people of New Brunswick alone every year by the increase, not in the through rates but in the local rates that were imposed by hon. gentlemen opposite at that time; and those rates have continued year in and year out. Mistakes may have been made in changing the rates on the Intercolonial in the last few years, and I am not here to argue to the contrary. The management found themselves face to face with this condition: they had to meet the demands and wishes of the brotherhoods and unions, and very justly give wages to the railway employees that would be in accord with the wages paid on otheT railways in this country; they found that their annual expenses for this reason alone increased by about $350,000; they further found that in consequence of the large increase in the price of coal another $350,000 was added every year to the expenses of that road, and there were other expenses which in accordance with the advance in price of all materials which had to be borne. Under those circumstances, they felt there should be some readjustment of the rates. This readjustment did not give satisfaction; on the contrary a feeling of hostility was caused, but so far as I know the difficulty has been settled in such a way that there is now little or no complaint along the line of the Intercolonial over the rates that are being charged. The people of the Maritime provinces do not want any undue favours at the hands of the Intercolonial authorities, or anybody else; all they ask is fair play. The question is, are the rates charged on the Intercolonial to-day unjust as compared with the rates charged on the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk railway, and the other railways of this country? The statement has been made to-night that they are less than the rates on those roads, and less than the rates on the Temis-kaming and Northern Ontario railway, which is owned and operated by the Province of Ontario. If that is the case, the people of the Maritime provinces have no complaint to make, and I believe that at the present time, with the consideration that has been given to the
new rates and the reductions and readjustments that have taken place, there is little fault-finding in the Maritime provinces with regard to the rates. My hon. friend referred to the taking off of the suburban service. I think that was a mistake, and I so expressed myself at the time. It interfered with people in Halifax and St. John and in places in Westmorland and York counties, who had been for years depending upon that service. The facts were made known to the authorities and investigated, with the result that those suburban services which were changed without a proper knowledge of the localities affected have been restored, and as good suburban services are now being given as before. As I said, in any transition period there is bound to be trouble, as was demonstrated by Mr. Blair's experience with the Intercolonial; but after a few months of operation, and when conditions become better known, these troubles disappear. That will be the case with the grievances that existed along the line of the Intercolonial some months ago but which do not exist nearly so strongly to-day. I think my hon. friend would have had better ground for moving his resolution some months ago than at the present time.
My hon. friend has dwelt upon the fact that men are employed on the Intercolonial who have been previously employed by the Canadian Pacific railway, and from that he draws the conclusion that the Intercolonial is being made subordinate to the Canadian Pacific railway.
That was not the only reason. I referred to the Gutelius-Bosworth agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think my hon.
friend is justified in drawing any such conclusion. As was pointed out by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, the Government at the time when the hon. member for South Renfrew was Minister of Railways, required a man for a high position on the Intercolonial went to the Canadian Pacific railway and obtained from them Mr. Brady.

Mr. Brady was not
employed by any railway at the time of his employment by the Intercolonial.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend may be
correct, but my information is that Mr. Brady had been an official of the Canadian Pacific railway practically up to the time of joining the Intercolonial. I do not for a moment think that because a man has been trained in one railway service, and to better his condition leaves it to work for

another railway that he is therefore) going to be disloyal to the corporation or Government who have obtained his services. Nor do I think it can be argued for a moment that he will have any desire to advance the interests of the company from which he came to the disadvantage of the concern employing him. It is not an unusual thing among the banks of Canada for a man to leave one bank to become manager of another, but does any one argue that this gentleman will be loyal to the interest which he has left to the disadvantage of the interest which is employing him at the time? We find the same thing in commerce. Surely it cannot be argued for a moment that because a man has been employed by the Canadian Pacific railway before coming to the Intercolonial that he will therefore, try to make the Intercolonial subordinate to the interests of the road he has left. I am sure my hon. friend himself would not subscribe to a doctrine of that sort.* If men are required for positions on the Intercolonial, and if it should be that there are not suitable men in the employ of the road to advance to those positions, I would ask where could you get better railroad men than those trained in the employ of the Canadian Pacific railway, which has been the most successful railway in the world and whose success is largely due and dependent upon the training and ability and loyalty of its officials? But my hon. friend goes farther. He could not, of course, ask anyone of intelligence to accept that argument, and therefore, he says: ' Just look at what was done in connection with the Gutelius-Bosworth agreement. That is conclusive evidence that Mr, Gutelius is playing the game of the Canadian Pacific railway and is not loyal to the Intercolonial.' If such is the case, I would ask my hon. friend what conclusion he would draw from the fact that the Canadian Northern railway were given running rights from Quebec down to Halifax at a rate far less than the rate paid by the Canadian Pacific railway from St. John to Halifax under the Gutelius-Bosworth agreement. Would he not draw even more strongly the conclusion that the officials who were responsible for entering into that agreement with the Canadian Northern railway, for the handling and transportation of freight from Quebec to Halifax, were playing the game of the Canadian Northern railway and were loyal to the Mackenzie and Mann interests to the disadvantage of the Government of Canada which they were serving.
The facts in connection with the GuteliusfMr. Hazen.]
Bosworth agreement, to which I wish to refer, are briefly these: The Board of Trade of the city of St. John, approaching this question in no narrow spirit, are. of opinion that the rate charged is not an adequate rate and that the agreement is not justified from the railway standpoint. They did not take the ground that the Intercolonial should refuse to haul the freight and cars of the Canadian Pacific railway from St. John to Halifax, or any other point, hut they did take the ground that if they did so they should do so at the proper rates and at rates that are justifiable from the railway standpoint, at such rates as the Board of Railway Commissioners would prescribe if a privately owned road went to the Railway Commission and asked for running rights over some other road for which rights rates should be prescribed. That is the position that was taken *by the Board of Trade of St. John and they made application to the Minister of Railways and Canals asking that the agreement should be submitted for the consideration of the Board of Railway Commissioners. The Minister of Railways and Canals acceded to that request. The Railway Commission were prepared to hear the matter at any time. The Council of the Board of Trade of St. John retained counsel, one of whom was my hon. friend who represents the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and the other the recorder of the city, and they placed the matter in their hands. But from that moment to the present, no application has been made by, or on behalf of, the Board of Trade to the Railway Commissioners to secure an opinion or a decision as to whether that agreement was fair and just from a railway standpoint or whether it was discriminatory against the port of St. John. The reasons that induced the Board of Trade not to proceed with this matter I do not know. I understand that it was considered that as the agreement was only for a few months, and as it has expired now, no good purpose would be served by pressing the matter before the Board of Railway Commissioners, but the fact remain that the Minister of Railways and Canals at once acceded to the request that the matter should be referred to the Railway Commission and the commission were prepared to give a decision in regard to it.
I have felt it only right to refer to this in view of what my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) has said. Different opinions have been expressed. Mr. Gutelius has asserted that from the railway traffic standpoint the agreement was thoroughly justifiable. Other gentlemen

have made different statements and my hon. friend from Westmorland has made a statement to the same effect hut at that time my hon. friend did not know of the rates which were given to the Canadian Northern railway from Quebec to Halifax.

That does not affect
the question.

speechtext:
That does not affect it
except to make it so much worse for the arrangement entered into by my hon. friend and the Government which my hon. friend supported because the rate was not an adequate or proper rate and not one which could be justified from the railway standpoint.
That does not justify this.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If this cannot be justified what will be said of the arrangement entered into by my hon. friend to enable the Canadian Northern to take its freight from Quebec to Halifax? I have every confidence that the difficulties which have existed in connection with the Intercolonial railway will disappear, and that the gentlemen who have been placed at the head of the railway will do their very best to meet the requirements of the country and of those who are connected with the railway itself. I further believe that all these difficulties which have been so often exaggerated and dwelt upon by hon. gentlemen opposite and by the press which supports their party will disappear entirely before long and that it will be found that the road will be run in the interest of the Maritime provinces and for the general good and welfare of the people of the country as a whole.
There were other matters that I intended to refer to but I think that at this late hour' I wiil not farther trespass upon the time of the House. I submit again to you, Sir, with all possible confidence that no case has been made out by the hon. gentlemen who have addressed this House in support of. this resolution that would justify the House in voting that the Government is deserving of censure on the ground that the methods of the present management of the Intercolonial railway are oppressive and unfair to the present railway employees and that nothing has: been shown to the detriment of their interests or that of the business interests of the country.

Mr. Speaker, if I can get the attention of the House for a few minutes I will endeavour
to (be very brief in the remarks which I intend to make. It is an easy matter to find fault with the management of the Intercolonial railway. It has been always more or less easy, but, in my judgment, it never was so easy at any time in our history as under the present management. My desk is full of various kinds of complaints against the way in which the Intercolonial railway is managed. I have reason to know that the desks of hon. gentlemen sitting around me are in the same position.
I do not intend to refer at all to these complaints. We, on this side of the House, unlike my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), who has just taken his seat, are not thinking of yesterday. We are thinking of tosmorrow. The question is: Can the Government of Canada successfully manage a big enterprise like this? Can the breath of life be put into the management of the Intercolonial railway? Can it be built up to be a great transportation system with modern grades, curves and branch lines reaching out for traffic in all directions where traffic is available and in this way become a real factor in the development of the great natural resources of the country through which it passes? In the past the Intercolonial railway has actually retarded the development of the Maritime provinces. It is doing that to-day, and the question is: How long will it continue to do that? The fact that the Intercolonial railway occupies the field has kept other railway 'companies out of the field. No company wants to compete with the Government. The de-12 m. lay in extending the railway to the island of Cape Breton is a good illustration of the apathy that has characterised the Intercolonial railway ever since inception. It cannot be disputed that the ninety miles of railway in the island of Cape Breton is the greatest traffic-producing part of the road, but Confederation was twenty-five years old before. that railway ran to the island of Cape Breton. Does any man -believe that any progressive company would have looked across the strait of Canso for twenty-five years without endeavouring to tap the resources of that rich and prosperous island? The first minister of railways to pull the Intercolonial out of the mud was the Hon. A. G. Blair. His successors in the late Administration followed up ihas good work. He saw that the Intercolonial railway never could succeed while its terminus was in a field at Levis. Within one year from the date on which the late Govern-

ment took office the Intercolonial railway was extended to the oity of Montreal. Immediately improvements began to be made; the road-bed was improved, the light 65-lb. rails were taken up and 80 or 90-lb. rails were put in their places; the Maritime Express was greatly improved and made into a modern train. Past freight trains were added toy which freight was carried from the ports of the Maritime provinces to Montreal on schedule time, something that had never been done in Canada before. Then again the Ocean Limited was added to take care of the tourist traffic. Shortly before the defeat of the late Administration, they embarked upon the policy of acquiring and building branch lines but they did not have time to develop this part of their policy prior to their defeat. It is true that this Government have talked a great deal about branch lines and the improvement of grades and curves, but it has all ended in talk. If they had kept their hands off we would have had now two important branch lines in eastern Nova Scotia, but the step having been taken by the late Administration, the present Administration and no Administration in Canada can go back.
We on this side of the House were much encouraged a few weeks ago when the views of my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) were accepted by the House, and we hope that this indicates a change of heart on the part of the Administration. The resolution of my hon. friend which was, carried unanimously on March 16, was in the following words:
That, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived for the extension of the Intercolonial Railway of Canada into the non-railway sections of the Maritime provinces within reasonable range of the said railway.
The House of Commons is supreme in these matters; the House of Commons has said that the time has arrived for the Government to act in regard to that question, and the House of Commons having said so, it is now the duty of the Government to carry out the mandate of the House of Commons, or else to take the advice of my hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) and make room for some more capable Government which will do so. It will not be denied that this resolution has special reference to a branch into the constituency I have the honour to represent. My constituents will await with a great deal of interest the action of the Government when the supplementary Estimates are brought down. There is no use in any more empty promises of investigations and of surveys; the only thing

that will count now is cash to be expended in actual construction. 'Even then it will be difficult for my constituents to forget that this Government cancelled a contract made by the late Government and deprived ns of our rights for three years.
The Prime Minister has told us to-night that there is an absolute absence of political or party consideration in the management of the Intercolonial railway. I am compelled to take direct issue with the right hon. gentleman on that statement. I will say on behalf of the Minister of Baihvays, whose absence and whose illness we all regret, that if he had his own way I think there would be less politics in the management of the Intercolonial railway than there is to-day, but if there are no political considerations in the management of the Intercolonial, how does the Prime Minister explain the dismissal of so many of its officials. A large number were dismissed in the eastern part of Nova Scotia, and in my own constituency there were men dismissed on evidence that turned out to be perjury; but the official has not been restored to his former position.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: How does my hon. friend from Guysborough explain the wholesale dismissals after the return of the Liberals to power in 1896?

I am not making the statement that there were no politics in the Intercolonial under former /management, but the Prime Minister has stated to-night that there are no political consideration governing the management of the Intercolonial railway to-day, and I am refuting that statement, and I say it is impossible for the Prime Minister to square that statement with the fact that a large number of officials have been dismissed. I have referred to some dismissals which took place in my own constituency, and I am informed that in the county of Antigonish, two out of every three employees on the Intercolonial were dismissed by this Government, and that some of them were replaced by men who were beyond the legal age.
Will the Prime Minister say that if the county of Guysborough and the county of North Cape Breton had returned supporters of his Government at the last election that he would have cancelled these two railway contracts? I question very much if the Prime Minister will make that statement, and if he cannot make that statement it is idle for him to tell us that there are no political considerations entering now into the Intercolonial railway management.

My hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) said that in regard to the branch lines, he wanted the idea to go abroad throughout this country that the defeat of the Branch Line Bill by the Senate is the reason why the Government were not taking over the branch lines throughout eastern Canada.
Did he say that?

He did. But even
though that statement does go abroad, the people of the country will not believe it because they know that numerous branch lines have been taken over by the Government and by the Intercolonial without any Bill such as he speaks of. What about the Drummond County railway, a large and important railway, in respect of which there was no general authority enabling the Government to take it over? What about the Eastern Extension railway, which became part of the Intercolonial some years ago; what about the Sunnyhrae branch and numerous others which have been taken over without any such Bill? In each of these cases the transfers were authorized by Parliament. It is idle for the Minister of Marine to try to spread throughout the country the idea that the defeat of that Bill is the reason why the Government is failing to do anything with regard to the branch lines.
There is another matter I wish to draw attention to and that is an interview given by Mr. F. P. Gutelius, the general manager of the Intercolonial railway, and published in the Montreal Gazette on the 23rd of March last. This interview was referred to by my hon. friend from Pictou to-night, and it was given for the purpose of explaining the purchase of United States coal for use on the Intercolonial. Mr. Gutelius travels out of his way to discuss other matters relating to the railway, and he undertakes to inform the public as to the most profitable section of that system. This question is one of considerable interest. It is always regarded as important by members representing constituencies in Nova Scotia, when we are asking for improvements or additions, or for branch lines, if we are able to show that the roads that have been built in Nova Scotia are profitable to the Government. I make the statement here that every expenditure of that kind and every branch line that has been built in Nova Scotia has been an excellent investment for the Intercolonial railway. Here is what Mr. Gutelius is reported to have said in the Montreal Gazette:
As far as the revenues of the road are concerned, Mr. Gutelius said there was no questioning the fact that the province of Quebec is the banner province as far as the revenue producing capacity of the Intercolonial railway is concerned. The money is made in Quebec, New Brunswick comes out about square, while the loss is in Nova Scotia, notwithstanding the statement made in a pamphlet issued down in Pictou showing the earning qualities of that section of the railway.
That is a very positive statement. Mr. Gutelius says there is no question about the fact that Quebec is the banner province as far as revenue producing qualities are concerned, and that the loss of the Intercolonial is made in the province of Nova Scotia. But what are the facts? I do not profess to be an expert on these matters, nor do I profess to know more about the revenue producing sections of the Intercolonial railway than does the general manager. However, I felt confident that the statements made by Mr. Gutelius to the Montreal Gazette on that occasion were not in accordance with the facts. I accordingly moved for a return to ascertain the exact facts as to where the revenues came from and that return was brought down a few days ago. It was delayed for some weeks, as I understand the information had to come from Moncton, and I have no doubt the return was made under the direct supervision of Mr. Gutelius himself. And, when brought down, it turns out to be a direct refutation of the statement made by Mr. Gutelius. This return shows that in Nova Scotia, with only one-third of the mileage of the Intercolonial, produces about one-half the revenue, and, instead of Quebec being the banner province so far as traffic is concerned, it is shown by this return that Nova Scotia is the banner province. It is also clear that this high-paid official did not know, when he gave that information to the newspaper, what he was talking about. With the permission of
the hon. gentleman, I would like to .ask if in the statistics he has prepared he has compared the profit or loss of handling the traffic in these several provinces. The bulk of the traffic might originate in Nova Scotia and yet that traffic might be carried at a loss per ton mile as compared with the other provinces, and no doubt that is what the general manager means.

I assume that freight
can -be moved as cheaply in Nova Scotia as in Quebec. I do not pretend that this statement that I am giving is absolute proof. It may require some qualification. I am only showing that the province of Nova Scotia, with one-third of the mileage, produces about one-half the freight traffic, and brings in about half the money paid for passenger tickets.

The hon. member for Westmorland pointed out that the service given by the Intercolonial railway was never worse than it has been since this highly-paid official came into charge, and that is absolutely true. My only purpose in calling attention to this interview is to induce the acting Minister of Railways to instruct this bumptious official of his to stop issuing manifestos in the newspapers and to attend to his business with a view to making some adequate return for the money which the people of Canada are paying him, and with a view to rescuing the Intercolonial railway from the condition of confusion that has overtaken it since he assumed its management.

I shall give my support to the resolution moved by the hon. member for Westmorland. I wish to say that I agree with what has been said on this side of the House with regard to the management of the Intercolonial railway.
A great deal has been said with regard to the branch lines policy of the Government and the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who is not now in his seat, has criticised the former Administration, and more particularly the former Minister of Railways and Canals, the hon. member for Westmorland, as well as the hon. member for South Renfrew, for the manner in which they dealt with this question when hon. gentlemen on this side were in power. I may [DOT] say in a few words that we on this side of the House have had to educate the people of Ontario to a realization of the fact that the Intercolonial is a Canadian railway, not the sole property of the Maritime provinces, and no person has given more devotion to that principle than the hop. member for Westmorland. May I be permitted to say that we in the Maritime provinces owe a great debt of gratitude to the hon. member for South Renfrew for the better feeling which he created in Ontario from the moment he took charge of the Intercolonial railway. It is to the credit largely of the hon. member for South Renfrew that it is possible for the Government of the day to acquire branch lines to be operated as part of the Intercolonial.
My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has made a statement which I am not prepared to accept, notwithstanding the courtesy which I wish to extend to him at all times. My hon. friend

imputed motives to the Minister of Railways in the late Administration in connection with the taking over of the Canada Eastern Railway. The minister seemed to dwell upon the fact that that railway was owned at the time by one Mr. Gibson, whose son was then a member of this House, supporting the Liberal Administration. I cannot allow that assertion to pass without refutation. The real desire was not to favour Mr. Gibson or his son or any member of that company; the time had come when that railway would be taken over by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company if it had not been acquired by the Government of the day. It would have been the greatest misfortune for the people of the Maritime provinces had the Government of the day allowed that railway to go into the hands of the Canadian Pacific railway, because it carries a great deal of the trade of the counties of Northumberland and Kent, being particularly valuable for the transportation of fish from points in Gloucester and Kent counties.
The hon. gentleman says that because of the action of the Senate the branch lines policy was not put in operation last year. Although we on this side of the House agreed with the members of the Government to accept the Bill as presented by the minister at that time, the Senate were not prevented from looking into the constitutional aspect of the matter. The Senate cannot be accused of partisanship in that regard. We on this side of the House agreed as to the desirability of the taking over of the branch lin£s by the Government, to be operated as part of the Intercolonial railway, but the Senate thought that it was not in accordance with the principle of the constitution to give the minister power to acquire and build branch lines without the . authority of Parliament. The people of this country to-day understand the duties of both branches of Parliament. The people understand that the Senate as well as this branch of the legislature should perform their duty to the people of Canada and that they were justified in introducing that amendment, which merely provided that the minister should obtain the authority of Parliament before purchasing or building branch lines. When that Bill came back to the House the Government refused to accept this amendment made by the Senate, although hon. gentlemen on this side were willing to accept it. It has been said that the ex-MinisteT of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) suggested that fMr. Turgeon.]
a conference should be held between this House and the Senate and, therefore, if my right hon. friend and the members supporting him really had had at heart the acquisition of these branch lines-, in the Maritime provinces more particularly, they could have -either accepted -the amendment or had a conference with the Senate and I for one feel that, in the exercise of my duty, I have to cast the bl-ame upon the Administration of to-day for having failed to acquire some of these branch lines. I am more particularly interested in this because in my county there is one of the longest and most productive branches along the Intercolonial railway, extending from Bathurst to Shippegan, sixty-five miles and from Inkerman to Tra-cadie, twelve or fifteen miles, and the people have been waiting for relief. We in that county are now subject to a double tariff; since the Intercolonial under its new management raised "the freight rates the Cara-quet company have also increased their tariff and therefore our people have to pay much more than they used to.
There is another branch to which I wish to call the -attention of the Prime Minister and more particularly of the Minister of Marine, that is -th-e extension of the Bathurst line -to the harbour of Bat-hurst. This question was mentioned some time ago. The Minister of Marine has given his support, when Premier of New Brunswick to the construction of this road. I referred to the line from Bathurst Mines to Nepisiguit Junction, four miles. The mine will certainly continue to be operated because it is inexhaustible and, much as I regret the cessation of business by -the Canada Iron company, I am in a position to say that arrangements have been made with the receiver by another company bo operate-the mines and therefore shipments will continue from the mines to Nepisiguit Junction and to Newcastle for some time. This line should -be taken over and operated by the Government. The traffic for that line is not confined merely to the shipment of iron ore. The town of Bathurst is well known to the Minister of Marine. He has encouraged the railway by giving a guarantee of about $15,000 when he was Premier of the province. I have done everything I could in behalf of that enterprise and urged it upon the former Minister of Railways and Canals -and -the former Administration had pr-actieally decided to build the railway and operate it themselves when the Canada Iron company suggested tha-t they would pref er to build it and operate it for their own business.' There is now a considerable lumber

industry there which would provide additional traffic. The minister is aware that a pulp and paper mill upon which $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 will be spent is under erection at Bathurst and it will continue to give trade on that line from the harbour of Bathurst to Bathurst Mines. The Government should build the rest of that line from Nepisiguit Junction to the harbour, four miles, which would make a saving of over thirty-seven miles in the transportation of the ore. I do not think it would be necessary for the Government to put an item in the Estimates for this season for the construction of that line, because the harbour improvements which I hope will be completed early next spring are not yet ready. I would hope that a survey be made of the balance of that railway out from Nepisiguit Junction to the Harbour, four miles, and meanwhile the department might communicate with the receiver or the proper authorities of the Canada Iron company. They have had a double subsidy, one from this Government and one from the Federal Government. The road bed is a first class construction. I ask the Prime Minister to take this matter into his consideration and I hope before long he will have his engineers make this survey.
I shall vote for the amendment brought in by the hon. member for Westmorland.

Mr. Speaker, it was my intention to address the House at some length in regard to the question brought forward by the hon. gentleman from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson); but in view of the lateness of the hour, I shall be content with a few remarks suggested by c-ertain statements which hon. gentlemen opposite have ventured to make.
They endeavoured to show, among other things, that the Bill passed by the House last year, making provision for the taking over of the branch railways by the Intercolonial, had not been effectually sidetracked through the action of the Senate, where their party is in the majority. The truth of the matter is that in this House that Bill was unanimously carried; tooth parties having come to an agreement in regard to the matter, the taking over of these branch lines was decided without a dissentient voice. It was the general opinion that such taking over was of absolute necessity in the interest of the Intercolonial, as well as of the province of Quebec and of the Maritime provinces. The matter was so well understood, that not a dissentient voice was heard condemning the proposal.
209*
To my mind, that would be an additional reason for the Senate to pass the Bill without changing a word, since no differences of opinion had been voiced in the House of Commons in connection with the proposal. It seems to me that in respect to such an important Bill, when there was unanimity of feeling, the Senate should not have taken the liberty of mutilating the Bill as forwarded from the House of Commons, in such a way as to render it useless. The Senate might have been justified in taking such a stand in respect to a measure which had been the occasion of much wrangling in this Chamber. But that was not the case as regards that Bill; and1 the Senate amended it to such an extent that the Government was no longer in a position to make use of it, and as a consequence the branch lines were not taken over.
It was even stated that the hon. Minister [DOT] of Railways was opposed to the policy of acquiring those branch lines, and that this was probably the reason why the Senate amendment was not accepted. Now the facts point in the opposite direction. I>t was the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) himself who introduced the Bill, who put it through the House, and that hon. gentleman is too much of a business man not to have perceived at once that this was a vital issue and of the greatest -moment for the future of the Intercolonial. There is, for instance, the International railway whose earnings cover ten times over its expenditure; the Caraquet railway which shows a handsome margin of profits; also the Chaleurs Bay railway and the Canadian-Gulf railway, which runs from Ste. Flavie to Matane, and shows receipts double its expenditure. So it will be seen that the Minister of Railways had no reason whatever to object to the taking over of these branch lines.
Exception has also been taken to the doing away with the train service known as the Ocean Limited, between Halifax and Montreal. On that point I agree with those hon. gentlemen, and I say that the said train should have been left on. If it was necessary to cut off some of the trains, it would have been preferable to do away with train services 33 and 34, so-called. There is not the least doubt that during some winter months, such as February and March, two passenger trains are more than is required. Undoubtedly the Ocean Limited is by far the most convenient for those who travel between Halifax and Montreal, and the people of the province of Quebec, especially as it runs by night. If I had any

suggestion to offer to the hon. Minister of "Railways, it would be to out out those two trains 33 and 34, and leave on the Ocean Limited.
Exception was also taken to the management of the Intercolonial. As to the condition of the railway proper, I am bound to say that, as stated by the hon. Prime Minister this evening, it is in as good condition us it was two or three years ago, that is under the management of hon. gentlemen opposite. But the criticism I have to offer, and the grievance which is complained of in my district, at any rate, is that the engines used in the Matapedia valley are rather too heavy and bulky for the curves to be met with along that part of the road. Whoever is acquainted with the valley of the Matapedia between Camptbellton and Ste. Flavie, realizes that those engines are ' too heavy and that it would be advisable to use lighter engines, as on some occasions those heavy engines have caused the trains to run off the tracks and inflicted losses on the Intercolonial railway. But all that does not affect the condition of the road, and it is as good as it was under the Liberal rule.
I noticed that the hon. member for Pictou charged the Government with being too lax in its repression of the use of liquor. It was stated that 'both an engineer and a . conductor in Nova Scotia had been kept on the service after some rather damaging evidence had been adduced against them. Well, I do not know whether the Intercolonial has two weights and two measures, hut I doubt very much the correctness of the charge, as, in my county, I know of two men who were dismissed for taking a single glass of liquor. I should add that under the circumstances I found the measure rather drastic, and it surprises me that such laxness should have been shown in Nova Scotia, as contended by the hon. member for Piotou. I do not understand why so much harshness should have been shown in the province of Quebec in dealing with two men who acknowledged taking some liquor. The circumstances are well worth stating. At Campbellton, for some time past, the disappearances of large quantities of liquor had been noticed on the Intercolonial, and steps were being taken with a view to finding out those who were guilty of these pilf-erings. A Moncton detective approached these two men, who were working on some engines, with a view to obtaining some information from them, and, to attain his object, he promised them on behalf of the officials that, should they give out information in their possession concerning these

liquor thefts, no action would be taken against them. The promise was made to them that they would be exempt from all punishment, and under such circumstances, as is well known, in any court of justice, the King's evidence goes scot free. Besides, those people not being under oath, were not obliged to state the truth. They admitted, in answer to the detective's questions, that they had taken a glass of liquor, and immediately they were dismissed by the Intercolonial management, in spite of the promise of immunity which had been made to them.
All that leads me to think that the charge (preferred by the hon. member for Pictou is without foundation, unless the Intercolonial has two weights and two measures.

Is the hon. member
in a position to say where they had secured those two glasses of liquor?

They had got the liquor from another man in the employ of the Intercolonial. That was the whole of the evidence adduced at the time. However, that was enough to put the detective on the track of part of the stolen liquor. What I find to blame under the circumstances, is the dismissal of those two men, after they had been promised exemption on behalf of the management of the Intercolonial railway.
Mr. W. F. CARROLL (South Cape Breton)-Mr. Speaker, at this late-hour, and as the question has been fully discussed I do not intend to take up much of the time of the House in a further discussion of the state of affairs on the Intercolonial. There are, however, a few observations which I wish to make. I do not intend to go into the question of the acquisition of branch lines for the Intercolonial, or into the question of building new lines as feeders for that railway, which, incidentally, would open up new country in the Maritime provinces. My views on that question are well known to the House, and particularly as regards the taking over of the St. Peter's road by the Intercolonial, and its extension to -Louisburg, thence to the mining distrcts of Cape Breton county and on to Sydney, opening up new country and giving to the mining people of Cape Breton county a chance to get lower freight and passenger rates than they at present enjoy under the system of railways which we have in that part of the country. I wish also to say a few words on the question of the management of the Intercolonial promoting men fsom the ranks of that rail-

illS
way to its high positions. I also wish to say a word or- two as to the advisability of this or any other Government buying coal for fuel on the Intercolonial from the United States or any other country but Canada, in view of the fact that we have as good a supply of coal for that purpose in the eastern part of this country as can be obtained anywhere in the world. I shall also say a few words as to the introduction of standard rules on the eastern section of the Intercolonial.
With reference to the promotion of men from the ranks of the Intercolonial to the higher positions on that road, I wish to say that neither this Government nor any other Government in this country has given that question the serious consideration which it demands. If I had time, I could show that men who have grown up in the service of the Intercolonial have obtained positions of the very highest character in railways across the line, and in the Canadian Pacific railway, and Grand Trunk in this country. The Premier has [DOT] told us that it is the policy of this Government to promote men from the ranks to fill the high official positions on the Intercolonial.0 I am sorry to tell my right hon. friend, and this House, that the Government is not putting that policy into effect. On the 26th of February last, I asked the following question:
1.	What are the names of the new appointees of the head office staff of the Intercolonial railway, since September 21, 1911?
2.	Who were their predecessors?
3.	What is the salary of the individual new appointees, and what is the salary of their predecessors respectively?
4.	On what railways did the new appointees see service, and what were their respective salaries there?
The answer was that nine changes had been made in the head office staff at Moncton, and the House will be surprised when I tell them that not one of those nine were taken from the ranks of the Intercolonial. Mr. F. P. Gutelius, previous to his appointment, was employed by the Investigating Commission of the Transcontinental railway, and previous to that by the Canadian Pacific railway; C. A. Hayes, who took the place of E. Tiffin, and who previously had a salary of $700 a month, came from the Grand Trunk railway and was promoted to the office at Moncton at a salary of $833.33 a month. H. F. Alward, who had previously received a salary of $3,200 a year, was promoted from another railway and given a position on the Intercolonial at a salary of $333.33 per month;
C. B. Brown, who came from the Canadian Pacific railway to succeed W. B. Mackenzie, and who had previously received a salary of $4,500 a year, was appointed at $500 a month; W. A. Duff came from the Transcontinental railway to take the place of A. E. Killam. He had previously been getting a salary of $250, and receives the same from the Intercolonial; R. G. Gage was appointed at a salary of $200 a month to take the place of E. A. Rolfe. He came from the General Railway. Signal Company of Canada. W. R. Devenish came from the Transcontinental Investigating Commission and receives $200 a month; G. E. Smart came from the Canadian Pacific railway and assumes part of the duties of W. N. Appleton, W. E. Barnes and Mr. Sharp, at a salary of $300 a month. Robt. Klock is the only person of the whole nine who can be said to have had any experience with the Intercolonial. He came fiom the Department of Railways and Canals, and probably had very little experience with the Intercolonial. So while the Prime Minister tells us that it is the policy of the Government to fill these high positions on the Intercolonial with men who have grown up in that service, I want to . point out as evidence of their not putting that policy into effect the return which came down on the 26th of February last, and from which I have just been reading. I take the ground that there are men in the employ of the Intercolonial as well equipped to	fill the places of responsibility on that road, either in connection with the head office * or any other department, as you can find anywhere on the continent of America; and there is no justification in the world for this Government or any other to go outside the Intercolonial to get excellent men to fill those high positions. I am not going further into that question, except to point out that all the chief offices of that railway which have been filled by this Government are occupied by men who had previous experience on other railways than the Intercolonial, and therefore this Government is not making effective the policy which was announced in the House to-night by the Prime Minister. I could go on and .point out further cases of men who have given their life's work to the Intercolonial-for a consideration, to be sure-good men, qualified in every respect, but who were overlooked in favour of men taken from other roads to fill places which they could well have filled.
In connection with the buying of coal

for the Intercolonial; I take the stand that *where it is at all possible to buy coal from the mines in the province of Nova Scotia, or in other parts of Canada, it is not good policy for this Government or any other government to go abroad to buy coal. The
15,000	tons of coal purchased by the general manager of the Intercolonial this year could have been obtained from the collieries of Nova Scotia. In the interview which Mr. Gutelius gave to the press of this country, he showed no justification whatever for going outside the province of Nova Scotia to buy this coal, especially in view of the fact that the 15,000 tons which he imported from the United States cost the Intercolonial about $1.25 a ton more than the Nova Scotia coal would have cost, and this at a time when the mines of Nova Scotia, especially the smaller ones, were working half time, and when some of their employees were absolutely in want. I want to point out another thing in connection with the buying of this coal. This Government has gone far away from the policy that any government in this country should have in asking fourteen or fifteen coal dealers in the United States to tender for the coal supplies of the Intercolonial. If these tenders had been awarded to the Nova Scotia collieries in December, January or February for the supply of coal for the following year the collieries of Nova Scotia would have been in a position to mine the coal which was demanded, because the collieries are not going to bank up their coal if they have no prospect of contracts in the near future. That gave vise to a lot of hardship and inconvenience to the coal miners of Nova Scotia during the past winter. If these contracts had been made it would have given a great deal more employment to the people who make their livelihood by digging coal and other work in oonne'ction with mining. The fact that Mr. Gutelius, bought 15,000 tons of American coal, though there were fifteen collieries in Nova Scotia, never even approached, to ascertain whether they could give the supply that was demanded by the Intercolonial railway was met by the statement that in 1901 coal was bought from the United States by the late Administration. I am not partisan enough not to condemn that act if there was no justification for it. But in 1901 there was a coal strike threatened in Nova Scotia and the managers of the collieries were not in a position to say whether they could give the Intercolonial railway a full supply of |Mr. Carroll.]
coal. Notwithstanding that fact there were only fifty thousand of sixty thousand tons of coal purchased. In 1907 there was no coal purchased from the United States but there was threatened strike then and there was an actual strike in the mines at Springhill which, unfortunately, became widespread in the year 1909. It was for that reason that the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals at that time was 'seeking to ascertain what prices would be quoted for coal on the other side of the line. But notwithstanding the fact that there was a strike in the Nova Scotia collieries at that time no coal was bought outsile Canada. I take the ground that no tenders should be asked for the supply of coal for the Intercolonial railway from collieries outside of Canada. I take the ground that where it is at all possible to obtain
1 a.m. a supply of coal in Nova Scotia coal should not be imported for the Intercolonial railway.
In reference to the introduction of the standard rules on the Intercolonial railway, it is true that the Board of Railway Commissioners issued an order to the effect that the railways under its jurisdiction should bring into operation the standard railway rules. But that has no bearing whatever upon the management of the Intercolonial railway because the Board of Railway Commissioners has no jurisdiction and does not take jurisdiction over the Government railway. Therefore, the order of the board has nothing to do with the rules of the Intercolonial railway. Some days ago I put a question on the Order Paper to the acting Minister of Railways and Canals as to why these rules were introduced and what their introduction had cost. The answer of the minister is as follows:
Standard rules are all in force on part of the Intercolonial railway and many of them in force on the balance of the Intercolonial railway system.
He also stated that there were as many as fourteen tutors employed by the Government to bring the rules into effect on the Intercolonial and that it had cost the management $5,000, the payment of these tutors, to teach men the railway business who probably knew far more about railway operation than the tutors did. But the most wonderful paTt of the answer that I got from the acting minister was this. I askqd him why these rules were brought into effect and his answer was:	To promote

safety on the Intercolonial railway. When the minister was making his statement in this debate to-night I asked him a question as to the	loss of life and the
number of accidents on the Intercolonial railway as compared with other railways of this country. What was the answer he gave me? Notwithstanding the fact that about four days ago he gave as the reason for making these rules effective that it was to promote safety, he could not answer the question that I put to him because he knew nothing at all about it. Therefore, when he answered the question I put to him as to the reasons for putting these rules into effect he gave the answer he did because he did not have any statistics to show that the standard rules had promoted safety any more than the rules which we have had in force on the Intercolonial for many years. He also gave the answer to my question that these rules had been adopted to promote ' economy and despatch in the operation of the railway,' Complaints have come, to me from railway men operating between Truro and Sydney, which latter place happens to 'be in the constituency I represent, against the introduction and operation of these standard rules. There are very many old employees who have served twenty, thirty, or forty years on the Intercolonial railway, who have been in the service since the inception of the road, who have grown old in the service, and who do not readily understand how to grasp these rules and how to put them into force, they having been brought up from their childhood so to speak, to the rules which ihither-ta have ibeen in effect on the Intercolonial railway. The result is that many of these old employees are unable to make themselves sufficiently acquainted with the standard rules to put them into effect on their trains, and they will, in consequence, be forced to leave the employment of the Intercolonial railway. The acting Minister of Railways and Canals to-night gave force to their contention by saying that there were some of them who were not becoming efficient in the enforcement of these rules. What is he going to do with them? He could bring in men from the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway who know these rules and who understand how to use them. He would place them in the positions which have been occupied by imen who have grown up in the service of the Intercolonial railway, conductors, etc., and he would place these old conductors perhaps in positions as switchmen, or something like that at very much reduced
salaries. I ask the acting Minister of Railways arid Canals if he thinks that is (a fair proposition to make. I ask him if, in view of the fact that the railway employees in that part of the country have sent him statistics to show that there have been less accidents on the Intercolonial in proportion to the number of passengers carried than on any other railway in Canada, it is necessary to introduce these standard Tules especially on the eastern section of the Intercolonial railway. What were the reasons which actuated the Board of Railway Commissioners in recommending the standard rules? The standard rules were recommended because in Toronto, Montreal and the larger cities of central Canada different railway companies were operating on same lines. In order to promote safety on such lines it was necessary to have uniform railway rules, but no such reason as that obtains in the eastern section of Nova Scotia, and no such reason obtains on any part of the Intercolonial with the exception of the line towards Montreal, and if I am correctly informed the standard rules have been in effect there for some time.
There are very many other matters in connection with the Intercolonial that I would like to discuss, but I will not delay the House at this late hour. The acting Minister of Railways need not come to this House and say that he is not receiving remonstrances from the railway men as well as from the patrons of the Intercolonial . railway in the eastern section of Nova Scotia. If he does not receive'such remonstrances he is the only member of the House who does not, because every member from Nova Scotia and from New Brunswick and from the eastern section of Quebec received day after day a list of grievances from the employees of the railway and from its patrons, which should be looked into by the Government. The acting minister told the hon. member for Westmorland that he brought this resolution to the attention of the House in order to make political capital out of it. Let me assure the hon. gentlemen that if the Liberal members of this House were only looking to make political capital out of the Intercolonial they would never have brought this to the attention of the House at all, because we have it on the responsibility of the editor of a newspaper in Nova Scotia, which is owned by the chief Conservative whip, that if the Government adhere to their present policy of operating the Intercolonial railway they will net have a Conservative candidate elected in any of the counties of Nova
331 n

Scotia through which the Intercolonial railway runs. If we were only looking for political effect, we would leave well enough alone and let the Government hang itself and defeat its own friends in Nova Scotia. But I think any hon. member of this House through whose county the Intercolonial runs would be remiss in his duty if he did not bring to the attention of the House and the country the grievances which exist which demand a speedy remedy. There has never been a time when the Intercolonial was more unpopular, botn with its patrons and employees, than it is to-day, and I trust that the Government will undertake to at once remedy the defects. I hope they will see to it that the Intercolonial is not run on the same basis as a company railroad, because it was never built with that intention. The Intercolonial railway was built as the people's road and has been operated as the people's road, and if ever there was a time when it ceased to be such, the people rose in their wrath and forced the Government of the day to a true understanding of their duties in respect to it. It is with that intention that mv hon. friend has moved the amendment which I cordially support.
